items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have to report that, accompanied by members, I waited upon His
Excellency the Governor-General at Government House on Thursday, 31 January when

items.speaker: I addressed His Excellency as follows

items.text: In obedience to Your Excellency’s reques t, the House of Representatives, in the
exercise of its undoubted rights and privil eges, has proceeded to the election of a
Speaker, and, as the subject of its choice, I now present myself to you and submit myself
for Your Excellency’s confirmation.

items.speaker: To which His Excellency replied as follows

items.text: Mr Speaker, it is with much pleasure t hat I confirm the choice by the House of
Representatives of you as its Speaker.
I congratulate you on your election to this distinguished office, marking as it does the
appreciation of the House of Representatives of your impartiality and ability.
I have further to report that I also addressed His Excellency as follows:
I humbly thank Your Excellency for your confirmation of the choice made by the House
of Representatives of me to be its Speaker.
I desire to repeat my respectful acknow ledgment to the House of the high honour it
has done in electing me to be its Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received the following authorisation from His Excellency the
Governor-General for me to administer the oa th or affirmation prescribed by law to be
taken or made by members of the House. The authorisation reads:
Pursuant to section 11 of the Constitution Act 1986, I, Lieutenant General The Right
Honourable Sir Jerry Mateparae, Governor-G eneral of New Zealand, hereby authorise
you,
The Right Honourable David Cunningham Carter
Speaker of the House of Representatives
to administer to members of Parliament the Oath or Affirmation of Allegiance to Her
Majesty The Queen required to be taken or m ade by every such member before that
member shall be permitted to sit or vote in the House of Representatives.
JOHN KEY, Prime Minister
Authorised
Jerry Mateparae, Governor-General
31 January 2013
William Robert Fenton
Hon Thomas Malcolm McGuigan QSO

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I regret to inform the House of the death on 10 January 2013 of
William Robert Fenton, who represented th e Hastings electorate from 1975 to 1978. I
7690 Obituaries 12 Feb 2013
also regret to inform the House of the death on 5 February 2013 of the Hon Thomas
Malcolm McGuigan QSO, who represente d the Lyttelton electorate from 1969 to 1975.
He was Minister of Railways and Minist er of Electricity from 1972 to 1974, and
Minister of Health from 1974 to 1975.
I desire, on behalf of this House, to expr ess our sense of the loss we have sustained
and our sympathy with the relatives of the la te former members. I now ask members to
stand with me and observe a period of silence as a mark of respect for their memories.
Honourable members stood as a mark of respect.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Seeing as this is the start of your term as the Speaker, perhaps you could
explain to us, because we are full of curi osity, the background of the regalia you are
wearing.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I can, Mr Peters. It was presented to me about half an hour ago, and
it symbolises in Māoridom goodwill, honour, and peace to the House.
Prime Minister—Statements

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, and in
that spirit could I just welcome you to your position here.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Shearer.
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that “There have been cases where
the Australians have considered whether th ey would help shephe rd a boat across the
Tasman …”; if so, on how many occasions has this occurred?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and one.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: From whom did he receive advice that Australia was considering
shepherding boats containing asylum seekers to New Zealand?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My intelligence agencies, and given that the member is on the
Intelligence and Security Committee, if he would like to have a briefing at the next
committee meeting and see the paperwork, I woul d be more than happy to release that
to him.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did he offer to take 150 of Au stralia’s boat pe ople, or was it
requested by Australia?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I made the suggestion. I made the suggestion for the following
reasons. In my opinion, firstly, Australia has much greater capacity to disinterrupt and
ensure that boats actually do not leave—[Interruption]—disrupt—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: —boats that would otherwise l eave for our shores. Secondly,
in my opinion, it would encourage Australia to keep boats that it might otherwise
shepherd across the Tasman and, thirdly, it gives us the optionality to send mass arrivals
that could come to New Zealand, if we so c hose to change the law,  to camps offshore.
All three of those reasons are very sound reas ons for the steps that we have taken. I
would also add that these ref ugees that we will be taking are within the cap of 750, so
12 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 7691
frankly I am somewhat ambi valent about whether they would come from Australian
territory or from Asia or Africa.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: When was the last time a boat containing asylum seekers actually
arrived in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I am sure the member is aware that we have not had a
mass arrival in New Zealand, but, again, I go back to the member and say to him that he
is a member of the Intelligence and Secu rity Committee. If he would like me to
authorise for him to see some of the paperwork that I see, he should feel free to read that
paperwork. I say to this  House that I have now read so me comments from Mr Shearer
that says he will not be reversing the Nati onal Government’s position if he ever gets
anywhere near office. He will “ring the Aussies”. Well, good luck! They will give you
the same advice that we have had: there are lots of people who could, potentially, come.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Has he seen any reports about a boa t potentially preparing to depart
Indonesia possibly bound for New Zealand in late 2012; if so, does he stand by his
statement yesterday about that boat: “D on’t know, don’t know wh ether, don’t know
whether it actually, actually, happened. It fell over.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot confirm the location th at the boat might have left
from, because there are intelligence reasons  why we would not want to do that.
Secondly, absolutely. I worked on that issue for a number of weeks before the end of
last year. I go back to the member. If he wants to—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Fantasy.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, it is interesting, actuall y, is it not? If th e Leader of the
Opposition wants to come to a briefing at the Intelligence and Security Committee, if he
wants to see the paperwork—hey, he should feel  free. I am more than happy for that to
be the case, but, by the way, th e last time this country t ook refugees within the United
Nations High Commissioner for Refugees cap under Helen Clark, we did not see the
Labour Party arguing about it.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Why has Dame Jenny Shipley not been stood down from the board
of State-owned enterprise Ge nesis Energy in the wake of her role in the commercial
failure of Mainzeal Property and Construction?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not believe that question in any way relates to the theme
of this question now being asked.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Although I am slightly
reluctant to defend the member in the corner, you could not get a broader primary
question than: “Does he stand by all his statem ents?”. The member is clearly able to go
to areas well beyond what the Leader of the Opposition has.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: My difficulty is—and perhaps th e Prime Minister could assist—
whether he has made any statements about the continuation of the Rt Hon Dame Jenny
Shipley in that position, and, if so, he mi ght be quite comfortable to answer the
question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not recall making any statements about her continuation. I
am happy to check the record—obviously a number of issues—but I do not recall any.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The easiest way to progress this ma tter is I invite Brendan Horan to
repeat the question.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Prime Minister has made
statements in the media about Mainzeal Property and Construction—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, and I am inviting the member to repeat his question.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Thank you. Why has Dame Jenny Shipley not been stood down
from the board of State-owned enterprise Genesis Energy in the wake of he r role in the
commercial failure of Mainzeal Property and Construction?
7692 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You will see the
primary question. It requires the Prime Minister to have made a specific statement about
Jenny Shipley’s position. The Prime Minister said he has not made one. The questioner
must now point to the evidence that justifies him trying to get it within the ambit of the
primary question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his assistance. On this occasion I am now
accepting the question from Brendan Horan, and I am inviting the Prime Minister to
answer the question. He can answer it accordingly, if he so wishes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I acknowledge that Dame Jenny Shipley is the current chair of
Genesis Energy and I acknowledge that she was a director of one of the Mainzeal
companies—I have not got that exactly off the top of my head.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Two of them.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Two—if the member says two, that would be right. That
would be about a hundred times fewer than the number of twitters he has made about
Russel Norman. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Sorry. To go back to the point, the situation is that we have
not seen any particular reas on—although we as the Government  very much regret what
has happened with Mainzeal, because that will  have an impact on subcontractors and
employers in New Zealand—at this point th at would suggest that  she should no longer
chair a State-owned enterprise.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is it correct that he went down to  Queenstown last week to fight for
the welfare rights of Kiwis in Australia a nd came back with 150 of Australia’s boat
people?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, that is not correct. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Interestingly enough, I did go to Queenstown last weekend to
discuss the deal that the Labour Governme nt did in 2001 to stop New Zealanders
getting entitlements. Phil Goff was the Minist er of Foreign Affair s and Trade, and he
stitched New Zealanders up. So I came back  with the knowledge and I pointed that out
to Julia Gillard.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he stand by his statement: “We are likely to create
170,000 jobs in the next 4 years, ” given that a year and a half later there are 22,000
fewer New Zealanders in jobs?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I stand by that statement. Secondly, there are a number of
different measures at the moment to look at it. The member is quoting from the
household labour force survey. But, just to quote from the quarterly employment
survey, which the Opposition was just a few weeks ago claiming as the gold standard
for looking at employment, under that measure 54,000 new j obs were created over the
last 2 years.
Infrastructure Investment Programme—Progress
2. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What progress is
the Government making in its infrastructure investment pr ogramme and how will this
contribute to building a more productive and competitive economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In 2009 the Government set out a
significant long-term plan to pick up inve stment in infrastructure in order to
accommodate a growing economy. In 2009 we se t out projects and funding for 5 to 7
years ahead. Among those projects where very significant progress has been made is the
roll-out of ultra-fast broadband; the near completion of the national grid upgrade; the
Waterview Connection and the Waikato Expressway roads are well under way;
12 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 7693
significant investment in rolling stock, ferries , and rail track upgrades has occurred in
KiwiRail, and there is very significant progr ess on metro rail investments in Wellington
and Auckland; and just recently the Government announced the first $80 million for
water storage and irrigation projects.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Why is infrastructure investment a priority for the Government in
the current tight fiscal environment?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It has been a priority, reall y, for three reasons. The first is
that when the New Zealand economy wa s in recession, extensive Government
investment in large-scale projects pr ovided many jobs and helped many New
Zealanders through that difficult period. Secondly, we want to get ahead of the curve of
economic growth, rather than having infras tructure bottlenecks as New Zealand’s
moderate economic growth continues. Th irdly, it has turned out that with the
earthquakes in Christchurch we have needed all the expertise and focus that the
Government has brought to infrastructure investment.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What results have been delive red from the Government’s large
infrastructure investment programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, there is any number of results. I will take you through
just a few of them. By the middle of th is year around 300,000 busin ess and homes will
be able to connect to ultra-fast br oadband, and around 1,300 sc hools and 30 hospitals
will have fibre at the gate. The first school in New Zealand to be built under a public-
private partnership has opened at Hobsonvill e. The new prison at Wiri will get under
way as the first public-private partnership, which will be a big step up in terms of
rehabilitation of our imprisoned population. And the Government is planning to build
more than 2,000 State houses over the next 2 fi nancial years, as we continue our efforts
to fix up the mess that the Labour Government left in our State housing portfolio.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why does the Minister think it is fair that New Zealanders have
to pay $1.5 billion more in petrol tax and ACC to make up for his Government’s
shortfall caused by low growth and uneconom ic spending on National’s highly political
roads of national significance?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The reason road-user charges and petrol tax have risen is
that in pursuing policies—for instance, those advocated by New Zealand First and taken
up by National 15 years ago—we have a dedicated road funding system, which is user-
pays. They pay for the maintenance of the roads, and they pay for the capital expansion
of our roads. And because we are spe nding more on a programme that everyone
supports, except the Opposition, which is against everything to do with jobs and the
economy, those charges have gone up a bit.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: How will the Government improve the management of its
substantial infrastructure assets?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Although it is certainly worthwhile to focus on new projects
and the funding of them, it is actually more important that we improve the management
of the extensive infrastructure that is alr eady in place, because, after all, most New
Zealanders will be using existing older infr astructure, not new infrastructure. So the
Government has set out in the 2011 National In frastructure Plan si x guiding principles
to improve the management of existing asse ts, and also to improve decision making for
future investment, to ensure that the billi ons of dollars we take off taxpayers and New
Zealanders to spend on infrastructure through PAYE payments every week, we spend
wisely.
Building and Construction, Minister—Confidence and Potential Conflict of
Interest
3. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
Does he have confidence in the Minister of Building and Construction?
7694 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why did he allow Maurice Williamson to continue as a director
of Holyoake Industries when he appoint ed him as Minister  for Building and
Construction?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As with all Ministers, I advise d that the Minister should seek
advice from the Cabinet Office about mana ging potential conflicts of interest. The
Minister, as I am aware, took that advice, a nd I am quite satisfied that he can actually
manage any conflicts of interest. I would make this point: I was advised also by the
Minister that Holyoake I ndustries does not have a cont ractor or subcontractor
relationship with Mainzeal.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Further to that answer, is it correct that Holyoake Industries
worked on the ventilation system  of the Supreme Court, wher e the lead contractor was
Mainzeal?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot confirm that, because  I do not know what Holyoake
Industries does, but if the member tells me that  that is the case, I am sure that it is the
case. That was the Supreme Court building that was tendered for under a Labour
Government, and the Minister was not the Minister then. And, by the way, 2 weeks ago
the Labour Party wanted Maurice Williamson to  be Speaker; this week it does not want
him at all.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he think it is possible for the Minister to manage a
perception of conflict of interest in his role as Mi nister by not receiving papers on
“heating and ventilation issues”; if so, how does he think the Minister will separate out
discussion of heating and ventilation from th at of other building issues, like windows
and insulation?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is incumbent upon Ministers if they believe they have a
conflict of interest, or a percei ved conflict of interest, to ma nage that. That has been the
longstanding principle. The Minister has sought advice on that , and is doing that. I will
bet, although I have not gone and checked, th at there were plenty of members of the
Labour executive in the last 9 years who had conflicts of interests, and they managed
them, did they not, Trevor?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has the—[ Interruption] Over here. Has he appointed a Minister
to be responsible for heating and ventila tion issues; if not, can the Opposition suggest
that Steven Joyce would be a very appropriate person to be the “Minister for Hot Air”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is free to suggest anything he likes about Steven
Joyce. All I would say is that  I would rather have Steven Joyce than 20 muppets from
the Labour Party forming a Cabinet.
Tertiary Education and Skills Training—Occupational Outlook and Moving on up
Reports
4. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : What recent announcements  has the Government
made to enable students and their parents to  make more informed choices about their
career and study options?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): Today I welcomed the release of the Occupational Outlook  report,
which provides a demand-side view of the current state of 40 common occupations in
New Zealand, their likely employment pros pects, and the qualifications required to
enter those occupations. The new report addr esses a shortage of readily available
information on demand, and a short to medium  term outlook for oc cupations in this
country. Used well it will he lp to lessen the li kelihood of people ending up in jobs that
are poorly matched to their skills and qualific ations. This new report will assist students
and their families to make more informed study and career choices, and it will also be a
12 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 7695
useful resource for employers, training organisations , tertiary institutes, and careers
advisers.
Simon O’Connor: What other reports has the Government released to help address
this skills gap?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Occupational Outlook  complements last month’s
Moving on up  report, which looks at what young people earn after their tertiary
education and compares what people are ea rning after studying different subjects at
different levels. It highlights some very signi ficant variations in earning potential for
different types of graduates. For example, top earners with a bachelor’s degree are
graduates in medicine, as you would probably expect, and they are earning around
$110,000 a year 5 years after leaving study, which is 3 times as much as a performing
arts graduate, while civil engineering gra duates obtain a premium in the job market
earning almost over $68,000 a year, which is about 48 percent more than graduates in
languages, literature, and sports and recreation.
Simon O’Connor: How will addressing the skills gap help improve New Zealand’s
economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, actually, I think addressing the skills gap is very,
very important to the New Zealand ec onomy. Through the Government’s Business
Growth Agenda we are focused on lifting New Zealand’s productivity and delivering
higher wages, and to do so we  must have a workforce that as much as possible matches
skills with demand. A comprehensive youth ed ucation strategy is about getting more
New Zealanders into education and training that  will lead to jobs. So, as well as these
reports, our fees-free Youth Guarantee scheme  at tertiary level, trades and service
academies around the country, new vocational pathways, funding for M āori and
Pasifika trades training, and the new New Zealand apprenticeship scheme all provide
great options to get young people into trades  and vocations that the economy needs to
grow.
Personal Explanation—Disclosure of Conflicts of Interest Regarding Banking
System When Minister

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I seek leave of the House
under Standing Order 354 to make a personal e xplanation in relation to the matter that
the Prime Minister raised in question No. 3 relating to me in his supplementary answer
to Mr Robertson’s question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: As long as it is certainly a personal explanation—

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, Mr Speaker, I do not expect to be questioned by
you as to whether it is personal.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: As long as it is a pe rsonal explanation, I wi ll put the leave. Mr
Mallard is seeking leave to make a personal ex planation with regard to an answer given
recently by the Prime Minister. Is there any objection to that course of action? There
appears to be none.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: From the period 1999 to 2008 I was Associate—and
sometimes Acting—Minister of Finance. A close relative of mi ne holds a senior
position in an Australian bank. As a result of  that, I gave Treasury instructions, and
copied them to the Cabinet Office, that I was to get no papers to do with prudential
supervision or with the regulation of the banking system. I followed that, and it is a
matter quite different from what was referred to by the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member.
7696 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2013
Climate Change and Economic Policy—Greenpeace Report, Job Creation, and
Infrastructure Investment
5. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: Will he implement the recommendations for jobs and economic
development made in Greenpeace’s Energy Revolution  report researched and co-
authored by the German Aerospace Centre—advisers to the Intergovernmental Panel on
Climate Change—and the University of Technology, Sydney?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: First, I am pleased
to advise the member that New Zealand is, and has been for some time, investing more
in renewable energy and environmentally friendly technology. For example, this
Government has a target of 90 percent renewable energy by 2025, and renewables make
up currently about 77 percent of our electricity generation, which is actually the second-
highest in the OECD. We have also impl emented and invested around $347 million in
the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart programme. However, the trouble with the
report, as I read it, is that it introduces massive additional subsidies and costs to the
New Zealand economy and would be disloca ting in terms of additional costs on New
Zealand households and businesses.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with the report’s main findings that New Zealand
has the right mix of resources  and talent to become a wo rld leader in achieving a low-
carbon, prosperous economy, creating new jobs and industries that wi ll deal not only
with the issues of climate change but also with some of the economic challenges facing
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I agree with him to the exte nt that I believe that New
Zealand has the right mix of talent and ex pertise to achieve in  a whole range of
industries. The Government has a view that the investment in industries is led largely by
the private sector, of course, which is placing its own money at risk, and that investment
tends to flow to the areas where investment  can be profitable and industries can be
profitable. The difficulty in actually trying to direct it away from those areas is the fact
that it involves very considerable cost to taxpayers, either directly or indirectly.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: That being the case, why does the Government continue to
invest in areas such as motorways, the roads of national significance, which
consistently—or a number of the projects sh ow—have greater costs than benefits and
also increase New Zealand’s carbon footprint, rather than invest in transport options that
would reduce our greenhouse emissions and reduce our oil imports?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, there are a couple of points there. Firstly, my
understanding as a former transport Minister is  that they have very significant benefits
over costs, particularly compared with some of the public transport projects the member
advocates. Of course, the Government is not just investing in roading projects. But I
will point out again—and I think it was addressed previously by the finance Minister—
that, actually, those who use the roads pay for those investments. We do invest in public
transport, but it is important to note that  those who use public transport, in many cases,
pay less than half the cost. There has to  be an ongoing subsidy. So I think you are
suggesting that there be even more subsidie s to transport modes that people do not use
voluntarily and, in fact, pay for voluntarily.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of the difficult jobs creation record of the
Government—no new jobs in 4 years—will the Government consider adopting a
different economic strategy, rather than the current one backing the mining industry, for
example, and actually look at manufacturing, a much larger employer—and particularly
clean-technology manufacturing—as an alternative, given that  so far the Government’s
strategy has failed to produce the jobs?
12 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 7697

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: My response to that is, firs tly, we have very significant
investment in this country in clean technol ogies. In fact, I could name for the member
any number of companies that are developing further and investing further in jobs and
growth in the New Zealand economy right now. But the member again seems to be
suggesting that the Government subsidise jobs in industries where they would not
otherwise occur—and that that is an answ er for economic nirvana in some way—and
actually move jobs away from industries wh ere they are prepared to invest in those
industries without Government subsidy. With th e greatest respect, th at is a recipe to
head the country to the poorhouse.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With regard to subsidies, is he aware that in his previous
answers and in the previous answers of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister
they have given us long lists of particular sectors that the Government is subsidising—

Housing Affordability—Initiatives
8. Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA (National—Maungakiekie)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to improve housing affordability?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: A major driver of housing
affordability is mortgage interest rates. Since we have been in Government they have
dropped from 9 percent to 5 percent, a 50-year low, saving a family with a $300,000
mortgage $230 a week. We are taking steps acro ss all five areas of land, infrastructure,
labour, materials, and compliance costs to tackle the doubling in house prices over the
past decade. The latest steps announced at the weekend are proposed changes to
development contributions that have gone up by 360 percent over the last decade.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: Why has the Government made a particular priority the cost
of land in sections as opposed to the alte rnative proposals of a massive State housing
building programme?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: We are particularly focused on the price of land in sections
because they have increased from $94,000 a section a decade ago to over $190,000.
This compares with an average section price of NZ$100,000 in the US. Reports on
housing affordability from Treasury, from the Productivity Commission, from Motu
Economic and Public Policy Research Trust,  and even from the Department of the
Prime Minister and Cabinet under Helen Clar k all recommended that changes focused
on land supply and section costs. None of  those independent reports recommended a
massive State house building programme.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What was the rationale gi ven in 2002 for widening the
powers of councils to set development cont ributions and for removing any appeals to
the amounts charged?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The law change in 2002 did broaden the powers for
development contributions and remove those appeal rights. The rationale that was given
at the time by the previous Government was th at the increased cost was of no concern
because it would simply come out of devel opers’ margins. Experience in the decade
since has shown that this was flawed thinking. The 360 percent increase in development
contributions has been passed on in section prices, and has adversely affected housing
affordability.

Job Creation and Unemployment—Statistics
9. Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere) to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment: Does he stand by his Government’s 2011 election
promise of “170,000 more jobs”; if so, why have a net 30,000 New Zealanders lost their

Employment): In answer to the first part of the question, yes, and it is important to

growth at the time—

items.text: —which was the Treasury forecast at the time, which I

the unemployment rate falling, from 7.3 percent to 6.9 percent, but it also does indicate

was lauded by his party as the best measure of jobs in the economy—which shows there

Skilled and Safe Workplaces programme, which we released late last year with some 50-

odd initiatives, including comprehensive programmes around vocational training,

30,000 jobs that have been lost over the past year; if so, will he step aside as Minister of
employment so that this important portfolio  can receive the attention and energy it
deserves?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am confident that I give this particular portfolio great
energy and enthusiasm. I would point out ag ain for the member that the quarterly

Rheumatic Fever—Vaccine Project and Prevention Programme
10. Dr JACKIE BLUE (National)  to the Minister of Health: What new initiatives
is the Government taking in the fight against rheumatic fever?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: On Saturday the Prime Ministers of
Australia and New Zealand announced a co mbined project to find a vaccine for
rheumatic fever. The two Governments will provide $3 million over the next 2 years for
scientists on both sides of the Tasman to co llaboratively identify a potential vaccine for
rheumatic fever that could then proceed to c linical trials. An eff ective vaccine against
group A streptococcus, which causes rheumatic fever, would be a major step forward.
This investment shows how seriously Govern ments on both sides of the Tasman are
taking this fight against this Third World disease.

items.speaker: Dr Jackie Blue
items.text: What other work on rheumatic fever prevention is under way?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: We are receiving encouraging results from the Government’s
$24 million rheumatic fever prevention programme in schools and communities.
Although it is far too early to confirm a decr easing trend, provisional data shows that in
2012 there was a slight reduction in the incidence of hospitalisations for acute rheumatic
fever. By the end of this year around 50,000 children in over 200 schools in vulnerable
areas will be part of the programme, which tests for and treats sore throats. We aim to
reduce the incidence of rheumatic fever by two-thirds, to 1.4 cases per 100,000 people,
by June 2017.

supplementary question. The Minister has not addressed it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I invite the member to ask the question again.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Did she read all of the relevant Cabinet papers before she agreed that
Novopay would be rolled out; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: All of the Cabinet papers, to  my understanding, go back to

and July 2012.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I think it is a re-run of
the previous point of order. The question was on all of the Cabinet papers. She has
indicated that she has read some of them, but she has not gi ven an answer as to whether
she has read all of them. Y ou might want to do a Dr Lock wood Smith and interpret she
is saying no, but I think she should probably say it herself.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I do not want to do a Dr Smit h, but I think, on listening to the
question—and we are all able to listen to the question and then the answer—by
implication it is fairly clear to me that the Minister has not read all of the Cabinet papers
dating back to 2005.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Did she read the paper that indicated that as risk mitigation the new
payroll system would be run in  parallel with the old system and that there would be an
8-month staggered implementation in five dis tinct areas, avoiding a “high-risk big-bang
implementation”; if so, why did she agree to a roll-out of the system  without that risk
mitigation being in place?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I did not hear the entirety of the question, but the
decision—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am happy to repeat the
question for the Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think in the circumstances that is fair. It was members behind the
Minister who made it difficult for the Minister to hear. I would be grateful if they would
also maintain a level of silence so the question can be clearly heard.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Did she read the paper that indicated that as risk mitigation the new
pay system would be run in parallel with th e old system and that there would be an 8-
month staggered implementation in five dis tinct areas, avoiding a “high-risk big-bang
implementation”; if so, why did she agree to a roll-out without that risk mitigation being
in place?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I read a range of papers, a nd at the time I was confident
that I had all of the advice that  I needed to make the decision  at the time. But, as I have
said, hindsight is a wonderf ul thing, and I took the reco mmendations of all of the
officials and all of the external consultants who were advising me, and I read the papers,
and that was the decision we took at the time.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Does she stand by her decision to sign off the implementation of
Novopay despite the fact that there were 142 known faults with th e system before it
went live, or before she signed off on it going live, that contingencies initially put in
place had been removed, and that the phased implementation initially proposed had
been abandoned in favour of immediate full implementation; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: As I have already said, I do stand by the decision in the
circumstances of the time and the advice th at was offered and the papers that were
before me in terms of the independent and ex ternal advisers who offered the advice. At
the time I considered it to be the best deci sion. In hindsight it is clear that better
decisions could have been made, but hindsight could serve all of us better as well.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Was she aware that the Ministry  of Education was considering
breaking the contract with Novopay provider Talent2 only 2 weeks before she signed

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. That was a very specific

items.text: My recollection is I did indeed  ask ministry officials what

Police Resourcing—Front-line Foot Patrols
12. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney)  to the Minister of Police : What
reports has she received on the number of front-line police patrols?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am pleased to advise the House that
police have reported a huge increase in the number of front-line f oot patrols over the
last year. The total number of police foot patrols increased by 70 percent in 2012, rising
from 40,918 in 2011 to 69,773 last year. Front-line foot patrols play a critical role in the
Government’s strategy of reducing crime. Th is means that there are more officers
walking on our streets, preventing crime, and protecting our communities.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: Why are front-line police foot patrols important to crime
prevention?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Foot patrols ensure that polic e are much more visible in our
community and act as a strong deterrent to criminals. Police are also deploying these
front-line staff much more strategically in areas where and at times when police know
there is a greater risk of crime taking place.  This ensures that the right people are in the
right place at the right time, and, along with the 600 additional front-line officers
delivered by this Government, is leading to large reductions in crime rates.
Teachers and Support Staff, Payroll—Ministerial Inquiry into Novopay System

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from Brendan Horan and Metiria Turei
seeking to debate under Standing Order 386 the Government’s announcement of a
ministerial inquiry into the Novopay payroll system used by the Ministry of Education
to pay teaching and support staff. The announ cement of the ministerial inquiry is a
particular case of recent occurrence involvi ng the administrative responsibility of the
Government. However, not every ministerial announcement will give grounds for an
urgent debate. The big hurdle to get over is whether the matter has reached the stage
where the business of the House ought to be set aside. There must be an element of
12 Feb 2013 Urgent Debates Declined 7707
urgency for the matter to take precedence ove r other business. I am not persuaded that
setting aside the business of the House for an urgent debate can be justified today.
There are two other occasions on which th is matter can be debated. The House is
currently debating the Prime Minister’s stat ement. The financial review debate which
must be taken before the end of March will also provide an opportunity to address this
matter. The applications are, therefore, declined.
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT
Debate resumed from 30 January.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Can I start by first acknowledging you, Mr Speaker,
in your new, illustrious role. I, like many of your colleagues, wish you well on this
journey of leadership. I also want to  acknowledge my colleagues who have had
promotions in the caucus and Government, and wish you well in your respective roles. I
also want to thank my other colleagues the Hon Kate Wilkinson and the Hon Phil
Heatley for your fine leadersh ip and service to the Government and, most important, to
the people of New Zealand.
New Zealand will be a good place to be in 2050. We might feel we are doing it hard
in New Zealand, but not only is it one of the best places in the world to be born in 2013
but we are also well positione d for the mega shifts taking place between now and 2050.
These are the words from the executive editor of The Economist, Mr Daniel Franklin,
who spoke at a conference last year and ended his speech by saying that with good
management and the right policies, New Zealand could come through the current period
of turbulent change in good shape. Dr Fr anklin’s comments about good management
and the right policies affirm the inspiring vision of the National Government and the
responsible and astute leadership of our Prime Minister, the Rt Hon John Key.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There is too much
background noise. Those who want to have pr ivate conversations, please do so outside
the Chamber.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. Dr Franklin’s comments
about good management and the right polic ies affirm the inspiring vision of the
National Government and the responsible and astute leadership of our Prime Minister,
the Rt Hon John Key.
The Government has four key priority ar eas. Firstly, to responsibly manage the
Government’s finances—that means living wi thin our means. Jacqueline Ireland, the
chief executive of Colmar Brunton, commented : “I believe that the recession and its
aftermath have forced many businesses to look at their costs and re think their strategy,
and those that have made good decisions ar e now far stronger, leaner, faster, more
productive and more agile.” It also mean s New Zealand earning  a living and being
sensible with taxpayers’ money. In convers ations with people—f rom the beaches and
camping grounds of the far north during the holidays to South Auckland communities
and market places—they just want to know that we are being fair and just as a
Government. In fact, in my conversation with  a leader of the Pasifika community he
said to me: “Alfred, we don’t want handouts. All we ask for is opportunity, and we’ll do
the rest. We’ll work hard.” They did ask me why the focus on the economy, and making
money as a priority, was so important to this Government—a ve ry good question. I
simply replied that in our communities, in stead of the word “economy”, we use other
words that have the same meaning, such  as “prosperity”—in other words, the
opportunity to provide for your family, to f eed and clothe them, and to help them
sustain the quality of life we have come to enjoy in this country. Most important, it will
help us pay our way in this country and in this world. They got it.
7708 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
Secondly, another key priority is to push ahead with the wide-ranging programme of
reforms to create a more productive and comp etitive economy. Albe rt Brantley, chief
executive of Genesis Energy, comments: “Wh ile the NZ economy has faced significant
pressure over the past few years, I am cautiously optimistic that this year we will begin
to see an increase in business confidence …”, which confirms Treasury’s Half-year
Economic and Fiscal Update of the economy growing at a rate of  2.5 percent over the
next 3 years.
The third key strategy is to drive better results and better va lue for money from
public services. Here are just some of the ta rgets. In the justice sector this will mean
45,000 fewer crimes, 7,500 fewer violent crimes, and 600 fewer young people
appearing in court each year from 2017, a nd also 600 extra police on the front line.
Education targets—98 percen t of all school entrants ha ving participated in early
childhood education by 2016, and 85 percent of all 18-year-olds having achieved
National Certification of Educational Achievement level 2 or an equivalent qualification
by 2017. Targets for social development—we began implementing our reform of the
welfare system to bring about an unrelen ting focus on work, including greater work
obligations for beneficiaries and more support to help people into work through a fairer
welfare system. And health targets—more ope rations now at record  levels. Thirty-five
thousand more patients get elective treatment a year unde r National than under Labour.
Elective surgery volumes have been increa sing, on average, by around 8,000 patients a
year over the last few years.
And, lastly, our fourth key strategy is to support the rebuilding of Christchurch. As
the Prime Minister said in his speech, out  of adversity comes opportunity, and as
Christchurch is an area wher e $30 billion will be spent over  the course of the next few
years, this is an excellent opportunity fo r the whole of New Zealand to support its
redevelopment. One of those opportunities is our commitment to train more New
Zealanders in vocational careers—particularly important as the rebuild of Christchurch
pushes forward. Colin James commented that the most important aspect of 2013 will be
the importance of jobs and bridging the ga p between education and employment. This
affects all of us in our families and even  in our communities. So what is this
Government doing? It is boosting skills and supporting jobs. There is a big opportunity
in New Zealand over the next few years, particularly with the rebuilding of
Christchurch, to train more New Zealanders in vocational careers that will set them up
well for their futures.
A week ago I was privileged to attend a celebration for Pasifika success in education,
and the Wellington launch of the Pasifika Education Plan 2013-2017, with the Minister
of Education, the Hon Hekia Parata, and my  colleague Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga at the
Ekalesia Faapotopotoga Kerisiano Samoa Church in Porirua. While I was there, a young

items.speaker: Samoan woman got up and said this
items.text: “I don’t like being called ‘underprivileged’,
because I am privileged to have supportive parents. I am privileged to have great
opportunities in this country of New Zealand to be able to succeed.” She went on to say
that this year she is going on to Victoria University, and through that, if she gains a B
average, then she will be successful in gaining a scholarship to Scotland, to the world-
leading university in opera. There were also the Tau brothers , who are twins, who
shared their stories of principles of success. Mafutaga, one of the twins, said this: “I
want to be fast like Usain Bolt, so my  principle for success is ‘Dream, Believe,
Achieve’.” In our communities our young pe ople are looking for these opportunities,
and what is the opportunity for success? It is their attitude.
So as a Government we are meeting this at titude of success. We have launched five
new vocational pathways that clearly signpos t the subjects that  young people should
take to prepare for vocational careers in construction, manufacturing, the primary sector,
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7709
the service sector, and the social services . There will be over 4,000 places available in
trades and services academies, and around 8,700 Youth Guarantee places. We are also
revitalising industry training to ensure that people have the right skills and training, and
that our system is responsive to trainees and employers. We are pa rticularly focused on
increasing opportunities for in-work training for all Kiwis by expa nding and improving
our apprenticeship training system. In resp ect of this system around apprenticeships,
being a tradesman and having come thr ough apprenticeships myself, I see the
importance. I have worked with tertiary organisations like Unitec and the Manukau
Institute of Technology, and I see the impor tance that these schemes and scholarships
have to young people in our communities. This is absolutely meeting a need and is
relevant for the young people and familie s whom we experience every day as
constituents in our communities.
Our changes also include from 1 January 2014 combining Modern Apprenticeships
and other apprenticeship-type  training under an expanded and improved scheme called
New Zealand Apprenticeships. These new apprenticeships will provide the same level
of support and subsidy for all apprentices, regardless of their age. We are boosting
overall apprenticeships funding. The current t op up for Modern Apprenticeships will be
redistributed across all New Zealand appren tices, as an extension to their learning
subsidy. In addition, overall subsidy paym ents will be increased by around $12 million
in the first year, rising over time. Incr eased funding for apprenticeships will allow
industry training organisations to invest in quality education for apprentices, lower fees
for employers, and encourage apprentices hips with growth. We are boosting the
educational content of apprenticeships. At a minimum they will require a programme of
120 credits, resulting in a level 4 qualific ation. We are setti ng clearer roles and
performance expectations for industry trai ning organisations, and giving employers
other options if the industry training orga nisations do not perform.  We are lifting the
profile and participation of  apprenticeships by giving the first 10,000 new apprentices
who enrol after 1 April this year $1,000 towards their tools—and jobs, of course.
In conclusion, just this month The Economist  magazine had New Zealand ranked
sixth overall on a measure of the health of society, from economic indicators such as
innovation to social ones such as inequality and crime. It is clear to say this: the world is
full of opportunities for New Z ealand over the next few years, and we need to seize
those opportunities with both hands. Thank you.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Is it not a pity that Alfred
Ngaro was not in the last National Party te rm in Government, when he might have
actually been able to influence it on doing something about apprenticeships, because we
had 3 years when nothing happened with apprenticeships. In fact, they went down by 20
percent. So Mr Ngaro can stand up and say to us how important apprenticeships are, but
the reality is that this National Government has dropped the ball and let New Zealanders
down when it comes to apprenticeship numbers . We have seen a 20 percent drop in
Modern Apprenticeships at the very time we  should have been seeing a Government
invest in the skills and the future of this country.
Just before Christmas, Campbell Live did a programme where a dog took control of a
car, and it was quite a big deal. I think it was a promotion for the Royal New Zealand
Foundation of the Blind. A dog was put in control of a car and it was able to manoeuvre
the car around. I noticed that when the dog wa s doing this, it actually managed to have
its paws on the wheel of the car. It had work ed out that the way that you drive the car
forward and give it directi on is to have your paws, or your hands, on the wheel of the
car. So a dog was able to do that on Campbell Live , but this National Government
cannot work out that if it is actually going to give New Zealand direction, if it is
actually going to take New Zealand forward, it has to have its hands on the wheel. That
7710 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
is what we have seen from this Govern ment. It cannot even keep up with the Campbell
Live dog when it comes to actually giving this  country direction, because it does not
understand that leaving it to the market —saying that the market will resolve
everything—actually is a flawed, failed set of policies from another century.
Times have changed and this National Government has simply not kept up with those
changes. It is never better exemplified than by the Minist er for Tertiary Education,
Skills and Employment, Steven Joyce—“Mr Fix- it”, or “Mr Fudge-it”, as we call him
over here, because he has been fudging the figures on unemployment right from the
time he took over. He is meant to be this genius who can come in and solve the
Novopay debacle, but the reality of his record in unemployment is appalling. For him to
stand up in the House today and briefly trumpet his excitement at the drop in the
unemployment rate to 6.9 percen t, and to ignore the fact that the only reason it has
dropped is that people have left the labour fo rce and that friends and families whom we
all know have gone to Australia, when the reality is that if we put those people back into
the equation and if we put back into the e quation the people who have given up hope of
even getting a job, then the unemployment rate would be 8.3 percent—8.3 percent—the
worst unemployment rate we have had since the mid-1990s. That would be the situation
if all of those people were in there. So that is no record for Mr Joyce to be proud of. He
cannot stand up in this House and claim th at he is any kind of “Mr Fix-it” when
unemployment is soaring like that.
Every single MP in this House knows about people in their communities who are
desperately seeking jobs. The people w ho line up for those supermarket jobs—in
Auckland the other day, 2,500 people were applying for 150 jobs. These are people who
want to work, people who want the opportunity to get ahead and to provide for their
families, and the complacent Government sits  on its hands on the other side, takes its
hands off the wheel of Government, and says: “The market will solve it.” Well, it is not,
and it is time for Government action.
It is time to invest in people, not condemn  people who want to work. It is time to
invest in businesses, in ne w technology, in a new economy. That is what the Labour
Party is calling for. That is the plan that we are putting in  front of New Zealanders. But
this Government has—

items.speaker: Hon Nikki Kaye
items.text: What plan?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Nikki Kaye asks: “What plan ?”. That is the question she
should ask John Key—“What plan?”. The Labou r Party has been prepared to stand up
and say that we are going to change the settings of this economy. We have recognised
that there needs to be a new economy. We have recognised th at we need to invest in
clean, green technology, that we need to upski ll people, and that we cannot afford to
leave monetary policy as it is. But this G overnment sits there wi th no plan for New
Zealand and no plan for the future of New Zealanders.
That was never more starkly put into focu s than in those unemployment statistics,
where 30 percent of 15 to 19-year-olds are unemployed—30 percent. That is our future.
That is New Zealand’s future. And even if  the National Government does not want to
look at that in economic terms, it needs to look at that in soci al terms. It needs to think
about what it means to have a 30 percent unemployment rate for our future generations.
What does that mean for our society? What does that mean for people feeling included
and feeling part of New Zeal and and our society? This G overnment is leaving that
generation behind. They are part of the forgotten New Zealanders whom this
Government does not want to talk about —the people whom it is leaving in the
unemployment queue, whom they are not ther e backing—and the initiatives that could
be being undertaken that it ignores.
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7711
This Government’s record in employment— Mr Steven Joyce’s, or “Mr Fudge-it’s”,
record—is unacceptable, and to put him in charge of Novopay just means that that
debacle will go on and on. Just briefly on th at point, this National Government’s shame
is in Novopay. It is wrong for people in my electorate to have to come to me and say: “I
have worked as a teacher aide and I have  not been paid since November.” How does
that feel? How do people look after their families in that situation? This is a debacle that
Hekia Parata, Craig Foss, and Bill English all signed off on when they knew it would
not work. It is a shame on this Government, and Mr Joyce does not have the record in
employment to indicate that he will be able to solve this.
I want to speak briefly about a couple of ar eas in my portfolio and, in particular, in
tertiary education. Steven Joyce has tried to sell to New Zealanders his brand new, flash
employment and apprenticeships scheme. Well, it is all very well  to rehash it and
rename it and put in place a $1,000 subsidy, bu t the lack of commitment to actually
working with businesses, to saying: “We’ll help you employ people as  apprentices.”, is
what is missing from this. It is the Labour Party’s policy to say to  businesses that we
will subsidise 18 and 19-year olds, using the money that this Government seems happy
to pay out in dole payments, to actually ge t people into apprenticeships. Yesterday at
the manufacturing inquiry in Christchurch a company came forward and said: “That is
exactly what we want. We want a Government that is hands-on, that is prepared to get
in and help us make sure that we have the skilled workforce that we need.” So to hear
about it now, to hear about it 4 years afte r this Government had the opportunity to do
something about apprenticeships, is a hollow promise from Mr Joyce.
The other thing I want to talk about is, wh at do we do to ensure  that the best and
brightest stay in New Zealand? What do we do to ensure we have the people who are
going to start the companies that will help create jobs? Well, in the case of this
Government, it is to say to postgraduate students: “We’re not going to give you
allowances any more.”
Over the summer break I met two people whom I want to mention: Anthony
Davidson, who is a student in Dunedin, and Tracy Merson, who wants to be a student
here in Wellington. They are two people who bravely put their stories into the public
arena to show New Zealanders what we are losing because of the short-sighted policy of
this Government to cut away their allowances. Mr Davidson wants to complete his
master’s degree in zoology. He is a person with a huge contribution to make, and he has
been told by this Government that it does not care about that. He is part-way through his
master’s degree, he has 1 year to go, and the Government has cut that allowance away.
What did he tell the Otago Daily Times? He is off to Australia. He is gone. He will not
be part of the future of New Zealand, because this Government is not prepared to invest
in his future and in our future with his education.
We have got Tracy Merson, who wants to b ecome a clinical psyc hologist. Clinical
psychology is on the skills shortage list fo r New Zealand. We import people into New
Zealand to do that job. Here is someone who wants to finish, who has been looking after
children, and who has been working and stud ying part time but wants to finish her
master’s degree, which she has to have to pr actise as a clinical psychologist, and this
Government comes along and cuts away her allowance, leaving her at the moment
unable to finish that master’s degree—unable to practise as a clinical psychologist.
What New Zealand needs is a Government th at is prepared to invest in people, a
Government that is prepared to give New Zealanders hope. New Zealanders want to be
proud of their country. They want to know that  they can have a future in their country.
At the moment what New Zealanders see is a future in Australia. They see a future
away from here. A Government that can co me into office, as Labour will, and say:
“We’re going to back New Zealanders. We’re  going to fight for the future of New
7712 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
Zealand. We’re going to give New Zeala nders hope. We’re going to do it in a
compassionate way. We’re going to do it by accepting that the economy must change. It
must evolve, but at the same time we must  ensure a fairer so ciety.”—that is the
Government New Zealanders deserve.
That is the Government Labour will offer in contrast to this National Government,
which has no plan and offers no hope a nd no vision for New Zealand. This Prime
Minister’s statement was nothing like a statement. This was the Prime Minister’s
whimper.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak in
response to the Prime Minister’s statement. I want to start off by saying that today I
want to speak as an Associ ate Minister of Education and as the Minister of Youth
Affairs, because I want to speak about young people in New Zeal and and the policies
that will make an actual difference to their lives. What we heard from the deputy leader
of the Labour Party was a lot of slogans. He  talked about hope and vision. But at the
end of the day, when you look at the Prime Mi nister’s statement, you see that there is a
plan for our country that means that young New Zealanders do have a future.
That plan involves getting back to surplus.  It involves ensuring that we have welfare
reforms so that young people do not grow up in disadvantaged households with very
low incomes. It involves ensuring we have the right policies in terms of business to
ensure we can actually create jobs. And when  we look at what the Labour Party says in
these areas, we know that its members oppos e everything. They oppose welfare reform.
They oppose many small business policies—everyt hing from the 90-day trial period to
Resource Management Act reform. The Labour Party opposes everything that helps the
500,000 small businesses in this country actually employ more young people.
I am confident that when New Zealanders actually step aside and read the Prime
Minister’s statement, they will see the ve ry strong contrast betw een a party across the
House that talks in slogans and this Govern ment, which has real policies in areas like
labour reform, Resource Management Act reform, small business policy, welfare
reform, and housing—reforms that are actual and that will do something for the young
people of this country.
I really want to start now and address the area of education, because we know that if
we want to give some of our most disadvantaged young New Zealanders the best start in
life, then we have to improve some things . Our Government has a very strong policy in
education. It involves accountability, it involves  raising standards, but it also involves
helping some of our most disadvantaged learners, and I want to talk about that.
I have recently been given responsibility in the area of digital literacy. We know that
as a Government we have spent hundreds of millions of dollars connecting schools to
ultra-fast broadband. I want to take a moment in this House to talk about a very personal
situation at a place that I recently visited w ith the Prime Minister. We went to Great
Barrier Island, a small isolated communit y, a community of 800 people. There are
children there who have never had the opportun ities in education, a nd this Government
has invested in that community to ensure that those children will have the same
opportunities as children in Auckland.
That is part of our vision for our e ducation system—wherever you are in New
Zealand, whatever community you grow up i n, you have the opportunities to have the
best resources available. Ultra-fast broadband delivers that, we have put several hundred
million dollars into that, and we are very proud of that as a Government.
The other point I want to make is that when  we look at education policy, the fact is
that our record is clear. We are spendi ng $9.6 billion—that is, successive Government
increases in terms of educa tion—and we actually spend more  than any other country in
the OECD. So our message is very clear wh en it comes to education: this National
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7713
Government, under the most difficult financia l conditions in a ge neration—the global
financial crisis and a massive fiscal imp act in terms of Canterbury—is spending the
most in the OECD, and that is something that we are very proud of as a Government.
The other thing we are very focused on is that  if we want to have  quality of life for
all New Zealanders, we actually have to do be tter in terms of the one in five students
who need help in terms of numeracy a nd literacy. We have, obviously, implemented
national standards, but we have also put more money into programmes to assist that. We
are also focused on accountability, and that is why we have ve ry clear targets. We have
got targets that are ambitious: 85 percent of 18-year-olds will achieve National
Certificate in Educational Achievement level 2 or an equivalent qualification in 2016.
What does this actually mean? It means that it is not good enough that there are
young people coming through my electorate office, and the offices of many of the other
MPs around this House, who have left school not being able to read or write. We are
saying that, actually, that is not good enough. I want to make this point. One of the
opportunities I have had was to visit many schools in this country. We have some
amazing teachers.
We know there is a complex ra nge of factors that we need to focus on in order to
bring about change. Some of that is about  having accountability, like targets, and some
of that is about having rich data and pare nts being able to know where to help their
children, and that is what na tional standards are about. But it is also about being very
clear about expectations, and it is about ensuring that we  have the best, world-class
infrastructure to ensure that students, wherever they grow up, whether it is Great Barrier
Island or Palmerston North, have access to resources.
We know, as the Education and Scien ce Committee demonstrated—and that was
cross-party, among MPs—that there are many ar eas of change that need to happen over
our education system. One of the key things  in the select committee’s report was that
our education system is rapidly changing as a result of technology. That means that
rather than sitting in a geographical lo cation, there are so many opportunities for
teachers to potentially reach students online in other parts of New Zealand.
Our Government has demonstrated—whether it is through our investment in ultra-
fast broadband, whether it is through the fact  that we will eventually respond to the
select committee report, or whether it is  through Network for Learning, which is a
major vehicle for the Government to deliver in  this area—that we are actually prepared
to put in not only the money but the policies to  ensure that we have some of the most
digitally literate children in the world.
That is something that we are proud of, a nd that is real vision. That is vision with
policies. But when it comes to the Labour Party, all we hear is negativity, slogans, and
opposition to policies. The point that I would make to New Zealanders is that they
should read the Prime Minister’s statement, and see the detail in terms of policies. They
should look at what we are actually doing, wh ether it is in the economy, where we have
actual policies about getting back to surplu s, whether it is through small-business
policies, where we have implemented the 90- day trial period and we have got a good
record on Resource Management Act reform, or whether it is through our education
system.
When you look at what we are doing in terms of investment in infrastructure, when
you look at what we are doing around Network for Learning, and when you look at the
fact that we have invested significantly in  Youth Guarantee—this is another area for
young New Zealanders. We are focused on de livering those programmes for 16 and 17-
year-olds who may otherwise drop out of school . As I have already mentioned, we have
implemented national standards. But also we  are interested in ensuring that, as has
already been mentioned, we boost apprenticeships. We know that although some young
7714 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
people may want to be doctors and lawyers, other young people have many
opportunities in the building and construc tion sector—which brings me on to
Canterbury.
I have had the opportunity ove r the last couple of months  to be down in Canterbury
and see that we still have a long way to go. But what I am proud of is that in the most
difficult fiscal conditions of a generation our Government has put billions into
rebuilding Canterbury. There is one area th at we have put a significant amount of
money into, and that is $1 bi llion in terms of rebuilding and renewing our education
system there. That is incredib ly significant. It is difficult and it is challenging, because
we have some very damaged schools and we have families that are still recovering from
the earthquakes. But again I make the point that we have found that money and we are
working very hard on the ground to rebuild that  city, and that is something that we are
all proud of.
The final point I would like—as the Minist er of Youth Affairs—is that there are
many people in this House who will stand up  and speak about issues that matter to
young people. As I have mentioned before, I think we have got some very strong
policies, and we have invested. But as the Mi nister of Youth Affairs I think it is really
important that we ask young people for their views, whether that be in designing more
modern education policies or whether that be about service and how we can increase the
amount that young people give back to the community, because that helps create
leadership. I am looking forward to the fact  that I will be visiting a number of
programmes in my capacity as Minister of Youth Affairs, because I think there are some
great community organisations across New Zealand, and there are some great young
people who are contributing to this country.
Too often we hear in the paper the nega tive stories about young people, but whether
it is Sam Johnson and the work that he did with the student volunteers in terms of
rebuilding Canterbury, there are some am azing young people in New Zealand and we
are investing in a number of programmes to help support that. I look forward to hosting
the Youth Parliament, which happens every parliamentary term—I was pleased to make
the announcement yesterday. But also I think there are a number of areas, such as the
Prime Minister’s Youth Mental Health Project and the Youth Crime Action Plan, where
we can do more. I am very proud of this G overnment’s policies in terms of young New
Zealanders.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I would be very cautious  if I were the member
opposite, Nikki Kaye, about using the word “p roud” in relation to this Government’s
record, and, in particular, about stepping into the fray of listing a group of achievements
and groups that should be feeling pleased wi th the contribution th at this Government
has made to their area. There were a couple that I just jo tted down; I could not even
grab all of them as the member spoke. But to list small busine ss as somehow being a
group that should feel grateful for the presen ce of this Government seems farcical to
me. Businesses are losing revenue, having to  shut their doors and go offshore or even
stop existing at all in New Zealand, because of this Government’s inertia on the issue of
monetary policy. Government members seem to  be the only ones who do not think that
there is an issue with manufacturing and th e productive sector in New Zealand. If we
need just a recent example, they fold their arms and sit back while contractors—
builders, plumbers, electricians—all suffer as Mainzeal collapses. They all suffer, and
on that side of the House they have no response to that situation.
The second group that is meant to feel grat eful for, and proud of, that Government’s
list of achievements, apparently, is young people.  Yes, that would be the same group of
people who are experiencing 30 percent unemp loyment for 15 to 19-year-olds, yet the
Minister of Youth Affairs had nothing to say on that matter. They should all feel
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7715
pleased that the Youth Parliament is comi ng to town and that 120 young people have
the privileged position of sitting in this pl ace, but what of the 30 percent of young
people who cannot even get a job right now? Well, I hope  that the young people who
come here for Youth Parliament do a bette r job of speaking on behalf of young people
than that youth Minister did in her first cont ribution as Minister to  this House. Thirdly,
we are all meant to feel grateful for the G overnment’s welfare reforms. Well, I have got
a bit more to say on that, but if the Minister  of Youth Affairs thinks that we should ask
young people about their views on policy, why do we not as k the people who are on
Government support right now what they th ink of the welfare re forms and how those
reforms are assisting them into work? I have got a bit more to say on that, Mr
Goldsmith, because I think we will find that welfare reforms are that in title alone. They
do nothing to help those people who are desperately looking for work.
The Prime Minister’s statement in the first session of this House demonstrated that
we have a Prime Minister who is willing to  allow his Government to recline while we
move into decline. We have gone from wo rse—what we had previously, which was
almost a “stand back and wait” option—to act ually almost taking a neutral position on
some things and almost a dangerous interven tionist approach on ot hers. It might have
sounded harmless when it came out of the Pr ime Minister’s mouth, because it almost
looked like a comedy routine, but underneath it a ll, whilst he makes jokes, people like
young people, the unemployed, children, Māori, and Pasifika are all suffering. As Grant
Robertson pointed out, these are the people who represent our future—the taxpayers
who will be paying for my retirement. I care about this issue deeply, not just morally
but fiscally.
Let me show you how this hands-off approach is hurting us. There are 270,000
children living in poverty. You can  argue, of course, that we have always had a degree
of child poverty in New Zealand—that is true . But we have moved from 15 percent of
children living in material depr ivation to 21 percent. Our social mobility is declining.
What do I mean by that? The ability of a child to grow up in a State house and become a
Prime Minister is lessening. It has become the area of the privileged few, and when I
say the privileged few I mean the baby-boomer s, not the children of today. We have a
number of children suffering from Th ird World diseases and preventable
hospitalisations. The markers are all there, but the action is absolutely absent from that
side of the House. Let us contrast that wi th the first speech th at the Leader of the
Opposition made, in which he clearly said th at Labour would present its plan on child
poverty to the country this year. We will do th at and we will do it with pride, because
we are willing to be bold. We are willing to address an issue that really speaks to the
heart of whether we are a country that s upports and looks after the most vulnerable,
because that surely is a mark of a society.
There is a reason why we need to do that  with urgency. I r ead an article in Idealog
magazine recently, where the writer said: “If the issue of income disparity isn’t
addressed in the next few years, our child ren will inherit a world of ballooning debt,
increasing social welfare costs, high unemp loyment, and rioting youth. Don’t believe it
could not happen here.” Yet let us contrast that then with what Mr Key said on child
poverty. Well, virtually nothing. In fact, whenever this Government is challenged on the
issue of child poverty, it responds by referri ng to its Ministerial Committee on Poverty.
I took a look recently  at what progress that committ ee, which meets quarterly, has
made. I could summarise it by saying “absolutely nothing”. If I am more generous, I
could say that it has produced  a few aides-mémoire, one of which is from the Ministry
of Social Development that list its projects that are focused on alleviating poverty. What
might those projects be? One was listed as the White Paper for Vulnerable Children,
which I can tell you, having read it cover to  cover, does absolute ly nothing for child
7716 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
poverty. Yes, it addresses some of the is sues around identifyi ng vulnerable children
who have been abused, but it does nothing to address child poverty.
The No. 2 project that the Ministry of Social Development listed was its welfare
reforms. I have read both bills in detail. Fo r both bills, I have sat on the Social Services
Committee, which has examined the welfare reforms and their impacts.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: With all that, the member should be more informed.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I have looked at the statistics, Mr Ardern, that have come out
since those welfare reforms have come into pl ace. Tell me what the measure of success
for those reforms should be. What would the measure of success be? Perhaps more
people moving into work. Well, on that measure, the Government is an epic fail. Last
quarter there was an increas e in youth unemployment in every single region—every
single region—bar one, and that is with th at Government’s fi rst round of welfare
reforms. What about invalids benefit num bers? They have gone up. Sickness benefit
numbers have gone up too. DP B numbers have also gone up, and that was a special
interest of the Minister for Social Deve lopment. She focused on increasing work
obligations, yet we have seen a decrease in  people on the DPB and in part-time work,
and an increase in DPB take-up—epic fail.
