What has the Minister also done, as part of her welfare reforms? Well, apart from
asking people to prove more often that they  are looking for work, she has increased her
use of sanctions. In fact, sanctions under this Government have almost tripled on
families with children. Across that time, has that improved the situation? Well, as I have
said, every single benefit bar the unemploym ent benefit in recent times has gone up. So
I would call it a fail, particularly when the unemployment benefit has always been the
easiest one to move people in and out of a nd the others have always been the hardest.
This Government, on every measure that you could pick, has failed on welfare, and yet
it prides itself on somehow being different and better than Labour. Yet we are the ones
who got welfare numbers far below this Gove rnment’s numbers, and we did it without
harming children nearly to the extent that this Government must be held to account for.
Welfare reforms should be about work first, and by that I mean creating it.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Then why are you so opposed to jobs?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I have received a letter just today from a man who has
applied for 360 jobs, Minister Smith—360 jobs. Our starting point on this side of the
House will always be that peop le want to work. It is up to  that Government to get its
house in order and do its bit by making sure that  the jobs are there. Instead, what do we
have? Some of the highest unemployment we have seen in recent times and jobless
figures that we should all be  ashamed of. Yet that Gove rnment sits and waits, and
reclines while we decline. Not on this side of the House. We have a plan for
employment, we have a plan for poverty, and over the 2 years we will continue to prove
to that Government and also to the people of  New Zealand that this is a party of hope,
rather than that side of the House, which is a party of desperation.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak in the Debate on the Prime Minister’s Statement and to the vote of confidence
in the John Key - led National Government. There are a number of reasons why I say
that. The first is that the National-led Gove rnment is the only political choice for people
who want to see a growing, stable economy that will create jobs for Kiwis—those Kiwis
who are focused and want to get on in life.  That is why our economy remains front and
centre for this Government over the next term  in Parliament. That is why we have a
programme ahead of us to improve the surplu s, or the economic circumstances to return
us to surplus, in the next term and a bit. It is also why we intend to spend the amount of
money that we do to rebuild Christchurch. It is also why we have introduced a number
of reforms in our time so far, such as the introduction of the 90- day trial period and the
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7717
changes to the Resource Management Act sy stem, and also why we have invested so
heavily in returning ACC back into financial sh ape. It is also why we have kick-started
the multibillion-dollar programme on infrastr ucture investment. All through that time
we have been dealing with three major challenges: an ec onomy that was left in an
unbalanced and poor shape by the previous Go vernment—it is interesting to note the
comments of the previous speaker, Jacinda Ar dern, in respect of unemployment, when
you look at that—the impact of the global financial crisis, and, of course, the
Canterbury earthquakes.
New Zealand has to become a magnet fo r investment by individuals and small
businesses—New Zealand and offshore. We ha ve to create business opportunities to
create jobs for hard-working New Zealanders . Without more invest ments that benefit
New Zealand, we cannot have jobs and we cannot have gr owth in the New Zealand
economy. What is it about th at that our Labour opponents find difficult to understand?
One is a prerequisite to the other, and there are no exceptions. The Government is
working hard to encourage investment through our Business Growth Agenda by
reducing costs and uncertainty for business,  and ensuring our people have the right
skills to contribute. The Government’s recent announcements on youth training and
apprenticeship courses aligned with industry, to best meet the demands to develop work
opportunities and training opportunities for young New Zealanders, have been
welcomed by all industries, but in particular by the rural farming industries. Our
apprenticeship schemes will provide the skills  and opportunities, particularly for people
in the trades that service the farming sector, but equally so in the farming sector itself.
There has been quite a vacuum in this ar ea for some time. So those announcements are
very welcome and will have an undoubted effect on the New Zealand economy.
For businesses to invest in plant and f acilities in New Zealand, they need to be
confident that they will have access to in frastructure, and that there will be support
through transport, energy, water, and teleco mmunications to sustain those businesses.
We have rolled out billions of dollars in investment in infrastructure over the past 4
years, which is supporting thousands of jo bs and will continue to increase the
opportunity for those jobs. But, unlike our oppo nents, we will not just throw money at
the problem. We are committed to fixing roadblocks like the Resource Management Act
that are slowing down the process and driving up costs. We want to work cooperatively
with local councils to reduce the amount of costly red ta pe. New Zealand has abundant
natural resources. The Government is taki ng a hard look at how our resources are
managed so we can continue to grow our economy and look after our environment. The
Government is working on a comprehensive package of reforms to the resource
management system, which will  be released in the next few months, and will progress
with our Better Local Government reforms.
New Zealand is a strong exporting nation. We are committed to increasing the
contribution that exports make to our ec onomy by aggressively pursuing more higher-
quality trade agreements. The opportunitie s in Asia and, particularly, the China
economies are enormous, and equally so in our Indian trade agreements. It is amazing to
know that there are members in this House who would oppose that type of progress, and
it defies logic why you might do that. Our primar y sector is an important contributor to
our export earnings. In fact, there is no other more important contributor—72 percent of
our merchandise exports. Access to water a nd to the primary production structures is
essential when you look at developing an economy that is sustainable. We are
establishing a company to act as bridging investor for regional water infrastructure
development, and we will invest up to  $400 million in regional-scale schemes—
regional-scale schemes to encourage third- party capital investment. Last week the
Government earmarked $80 million for the ini tial stages of the company’s operations,
7718 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
and that will be set aside in the 2013 Budget. Reliable irrigation presents a major step in
unlocking economic potential for New Zeal and. Having our tradable sectors grow
strongly, delivering on the Government’s economic growth goals, is the No. 1 objective
of this Government.
I hope that the rural and provi ncial New Zealanders who ar e listening to this debate,
and others who may listen in on future de bates, take note of what our opponents are
saying. For example, the Leader of the Opposi tion stated in his speech to the nation that
“The reality is that we will not create more better paying jobs by simply exporting more
milk powder.” How wrong is that! How naive a nd ignorant is that! How far off course
can you be? Some of the very high-e nd, sophisticated nu traceuticals and
pharmaceuticals and high-end food ingredient po wders that are now processed in some
of the largest manufacturing processing sites in the world here in our dairy industry hold
one of the strongest keys to extra growth in this economy. And that can be done in a
very sustainable, clean, green way. When you look at what the Leader of the Opposition
is proposing, he is proposing an increase in industry. That is not a bad thing. In fact,
increases in industry will generally lead to  more jobs and more exports. But you are
talking about the industrialisation of New Zealand in terms of its economy. What effects
would that have on the environment? What  sorts of effects do you create in the
environment when you surge forward entirely focused on the industrial area, as opposed
to agriculture? Measure it credib ly and sensibly against the e ffects of agriculture, and I
would suggest that the effects on the environment are far more.
Labour has not changed its ideology since the 1980s, when the then Prime Minister,
David Lange, described agriculture as a sunset industry. So 71 percent of our
merchandise export earnings are a sunset industry. Well, certainly under Labour they
would be, because its vision for the New Z ealand economy is a capital gains tax, higher
income tax, higher company tax, an emission s trading tax, no support for irrigation
systems, higher ACC levies, no more 90-day trial periods for employment, rural New
Zealand stuck in a dial-up age, less road  construction, more unproductive spending, and
more debt. Is there any mix of policies that could be more of a contrast, more backward-
looking, and less likely to grow the New Zealand economy than those? And it gets
worse, because, for Labour to be in Gove rnment, it would have to coalesce with the
Greens. Let us just have a look at what the Greens have said. They would go harder than
Labour on the emissions trading tax. They would put a restriction on livestock numbers.
They would put a restriction on water use. They would put  a restrictio n on nitrogen
applications. The comparison is black a nd white, and clearly it does not favour a
Labour, Green, and who-knows-who coalition Government.
If you think that by living in an urban environment in your house in Auckland or
Wellington you are safe from these changes,  then I would suggest you think again,
because if our agricultural sector does not  prosper and grow, then nor will our urban
areas. It is that simple. Seventy-one per cent of our merchandise exports from this
sector—

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Where are the jobs? In the cities.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: Well, the agricultural sector is the highest employer, both
directly and indirectly in New Zealand. I sugge st that a change of Government at this
stage would be devastating to the New Zealand economy. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: First in this reply to the Prime Minister’s
statement I would like to extend my congratul ations to Mr Speaker on his ascension to
that throne. I hope he enjoys the position. If he does not, I understand there is a vacancy
coming up in Rome towards the end of the year  and he might find that of some interest.
But I hope he also takes the opportunity to review conventions and definitions and to
make his own imprint on the House. I wish him well.
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7719
In reply to the Prime Minister’s speech, I want to spend some time going to the heart
of people’s needs, and that is their health a nd the health of their children. In his speech
in this debate 2 weeks ago the Minister  of Health, Tony Ryall, trumpeted his
Government’s so-called successe s in health. He trotted out the things he usually trots
out: more doctors and nurses—although those figures have been roundly disputed and
comprehensively debunked by the Association of  Salaried Medical Specialists, together
with the Minister’s own ministry—and he  talked about more elective surgical
procedures. Those are the things that one gets  when one pays the district health boards
to provide them. These are the easy wins, wh ich is what this Minister focuses on. But
what are the statistics that the Minister of  Health hides from? First of all, 3,701 more
children were admitted to hospital last year  than the year before. Nearly 4,000 more
children with preventable respiratory infections, preventable skin infections, and even
some vaccine-preventable diseases were admitted to our hospitals around New Zealand
last year than in 2011. This is not what success looks like; this is what failure looks like.
For every 100 P ākehā children admitted to hospital there were 156 M āori children
admitted, and a staggering 251 Pacific Island chil dren admitted. This is not a successful
health system; this is a failing health system. Health inequalities, such as those that are
demonstrated by the admission of children to hospitals, equal a bleaker future for our
children and not National’s much-vaunted brighter one.
Health targets are, by and large, a good idea. We introdu ced them when we were in
Government, and this Government has continued them. But they need constant revision.
I want to refer to a particular example that has come to my attention in recent times. An
ophthalmologist was to operate on a sma ll boy who had a genetic but surgically
correctable sight problem. The boy was booked in for surger y on a Thursday afternoon,
I think it was. At the last minute the ophthalm ologist had to cancel that boy’s operation
because the hospital needed to do two cataract op erations in that period in order to meet
its elective surgical targets. In other word s, the number crunchers came before that
specialist’s clinical decision on who was the priority for surgery that afternoon. When
we see this kind of thing happening in our hospitals we know that the health targets,
which the Minister is trumpeting on a daily basi s, are in fact distorting the delivery of
health services and not improving them. In that  story the specialist told me that he felt
demoralised—demoralised by the compulsion to cance l that little boy’s surgery so that
he could do two much quicker cataract operat ions in its place, in order to meet the
Minister’s elective surgery ta rgets. These are targets gone mad, if that is what is
happening. I understand that this is not an isolated incident . So, although the Minister
wants to get up and talk about particularly el ective surgical procedur e targets, then let
him also say to this House what has to be cut in order to allow hospitals to meet those
targets.
Let me give another example. At Countie s Manukau District Health Board it takes
now, depending on who you talk to, somewhere between 2 weeks and 8 weeks to get a
hip operation—at Counties Manukau it takes be tween 2 weeks and 8 weeks to get a hip
operation. It has almost got to the stage where it is going out into the highways and
byways seeking out the halt, the lame, and the blind—let us throw in some cataract
operations as well—and saying “Have you got a dodgy hip? I have got  a deal for you.”
If that is not skewing the purpose of health targets, I do not know what is. In fact,
recently the Government was reported to be eyeing axing some of the elective surgical
procedures on the basis of some advice fr om the National Health Committee, which
comprises people for whom I have a great de al of respect. However, the particular
procedure that it identified as possibly being one of the ones that could be taken out was
the insertion of grommets. The insertion of  grommets for children—babies, usually;
infants with ear infections—sets them up to be  able to hear properl y, to get past their
7720 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
glue ear or their otitis medi a infection, which causes them not to be able to hear, and
then paves the way for them to learn at school , to be responsive to their environment,
and to not be problematic. This  Minister is compelling advice to be brought to him—he
is compelling advice that he wants to hear. In other words, whatever you do, do not cut
elective surgery to people who can vote. Do not cut elective surgery to the elderly, but
go and ahead and sacrifice elective surgical procedures for children, because they do not
vote. This cynical approach to the delivery of health care is the hallmark of this Minister
and needs to be stopped. It is time to revise these health targets.
Children’s health is our best investment. Nearly 4,000 more admissions to hospital of
children with preventable or poverty-related diseases in 2012 than in 2011 is not success
in the health system; it is failure. This Government is failing our children. Housing is
one of the keys to this, and this Government has done nothing in 4 years, now in its fifth
year, to improve health inequalities that st em from poor housing. This Government also
has a black hole where its plan for an agei ng population should be. This is not success;
it is failure. For all of Tony Ryall’s shovelling of negative qu estions off to other lesser
mortals in his caucus, people are now seei ng beyond this teflon veneer and the evidence
of failure is piling up. Child poverty is some thing that needs to be addressed. Health
intervention can stem the worst impacts of child  poverty, but it is not a cure in itself. So
the Minister of Health needs to get alongside the Minister of Housing and say “How can
we knit our policies together so  that they give our childre n the best chance?”. Opposing
a decent living wage and opposing realistic mi nimum wage increases year on year are
the things that will not improve the health of our children in this country. They will only
make it worse. The Government is not a success; it is a failure.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, it w ould be churlish of me
not to congratulate the new Speaker, so I will congratulate the new Speaker on taking
my job. I am sure that the new Speaker will do a fantastic job. He has been in the job
really only 1 day and already he is making his mark on the House.
I want to cut to the chase. In 2014 this c ountry goes to a general election. From an
article today a member of this House is quoted as saying: “I will not stand by while [his
daughters’] rights and freedoms of other New Zealanders and Westerners, are
denigrated by a sorry pack of  misogynist troglodytes from Wogistan.” That is what one
of these MPs said today.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Disgraceful!

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: It is disgraceful, it is shamef ul, it is racist, and I have never
heard—never ever heard—something worse than that come out of th e mouth of one of
the MPs in my time in the House. Yes, we have come close to it; I will own up to that.
But never ever—never ever—have we come even to the verge of bei ng racist. I want to
say this and to put out, I suppose, a challenge to everybody in this House not only that
they say they dislike or are ashamed of that sort of talk but also that they would distance
their party from being in a coalition—in a coalition—with that member’s party.
I know for a fact that that sort of langua ge would not come out of the mouth of
members of New Zealand First, except for one. He has done it before, so it is no
surprise. It would have been a surprise if Andrew Williams had said that. It would have
been a surprise if somebody else had said that. But it was Ri chard Prosser, I am sorry to
say.
You know, there is a price to pay for living in paradise. But it is not a paradise if the
Government is going to be Labour, Green, and New Zealand First. So I call on the
Green Party and the Labour Pa rty to distance themselves now  from being in a coalition
with a member who thinks and actually speaks like that in public.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: They won’t.
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7721

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: I do not know whether they will or not. You know, in
something like 22 months’ time we go to an  election, and all we can hear from the
pretenders—and in saying this, I will most pr obably put some of my colleagues off me;
well, maybe put more colleagues off me. But at least the Greens actually believe in what
they say. They come to this House with a purpose and to see a w hole lot of changes,
which they talk about incessantly. I know that upsets us, but I kind of like that.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: They won’t have you, mate.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: On the other hand—no, they will not have me! On the other
hand we have the New Zealand Labour Party. All we get from the Labour Party, and
from Trevor Mallard, is—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Oh! Let it go.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: “Oh!”, he says, “Oh!”. Mr Faafoi  says “Oh!”. Well, here it is
in black and white for Mr Faafoi from Pori rua: “Stop thrashing dead horse and work on
imaginative tools appropriate for New Zealand.”  I have not heard something better than
that from Russel Norman. It is about findi ng the tools that are appropriate for New
Zealand. All Mr Mallard can come back and say—well, I do not want to go there. You
know, what we are seeing is a party bereft. I mean the New Zealand Labour Party. I am
not attacking the Green Party, because it believes in the stuff that it trots out.
I want to talk about housing, just for a minute. The New Zeala nd Labour Party has
promised us 300,000—is it 300,000 homes, or is 100,000 homes—

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: —100,000 homes, at under $300,000 each, over 10 years.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: That’s roughly.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Did you hear that? It was very  quiet. It was very quiet—
“roughly”. It was “roughly” $300,000. Well, here  is the thing: I was brought up, born
and bred, in Ōtara. For those in Ōtara, and for those in Porirua, Freemans Bay, Kaiti,
Tikipunga, all—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: How affordable is Freemans Bay now, Tau?

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Well, I do not know. I live on the peninsula. I am not looking
for a home in Freemans Bay at the moment. Here is the thing: if you want people to live
in houses that are purchased or valued at under $300k a year , then all you are going to
do is build more slums, ghettos, and poor  neighbourhoods like the one that I was
brought up in, because all the houses were the same. They were all the same—little
boxes made of ticky-tacky. Alt hough it suited the Labour Part y to have those policies,
although it suited my mother and father while  bringing up four children, and although it
suited my neighbours to do the same, all it di d was push the problem into one area. And
now why do you think that South Auckland is a bit of a mess? Why do you think—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Why are you selling Housing New Zealand stock?

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: No, no, sorry, I am not going to listen to it any more. I am not
listening to it any more.

items.speaker: Here is the thing
items.text: one person—one pe rson—from the Labour members actually
comes out of Ōtara, and that is William Sio. In fact, he and I were in the same class.
Admittedly, I was a year in front of him, and that was second-year fifth. But here is the
rub. Here is the rub. Those people over th ere talk on behalf of the poor and the
downtrodden. What a load of rubbish! What a load of rubbish! They should try to be
downtrodden, try to be underprivileged, for a change. All those people across the way
have gone to university, and have gone stra ight from university into a job—oh, that is
right—as a member of Parliament. And if th ey did have a job be forehand, it was with
the unions. It was with the unions. I did it differently: I went from the unions to the
National Party.
7722 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
I want to say, in the 2 minutes that I have got left, that I have immense faith in the
Hon Dr Nick Smith as the new Minister of Housing, because in his mind there are ways
and means to make housing affordable, and I h ope that one of my ideas gets a bit of a
run. That is, you know in the old days—in th e days of my mother and father—it was
easy for them to actually put a dwelling on the back of their property, and to have that
dwelling for themselves, with no cross- leasing fees, no development fund for a
developer, and certainly no Resource Manage ment Act to get in the way. You are not
allowed to do that these days. It is at least $100,000 more to cross-lease and to build—

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: It’s called slum, infill housing.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Oh, infill housing. Well, we cannot all have a 10-acre lifestyle
block full of lemon trees, Mr Andrew Williams. We cannot have that, but the fact is that
there are things that we can do to make it better for young people trying to get their
dream home, especially on the Te Atatū peninsula—just like Phil Twyford. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Is some member seeking th e call, because I might have
to put the question. I understand it is a Green call, but if those members are not taking
it—Dr Calder.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: As the World Economic Forum came to a close a
few days ago in Davos, IMF chief Christine Lagarde enjoined the Governments of the
world to remain focused. She counselled countries to adopt the “do not relax” principle.
The IMF forecast is for very fragile a nd timid growth for 2013, based on nations
making the right decisions. One could argue th at the international system is undergoing
a generational transformation. Although some speakers’ minds at Davos seemed to be
eased by the US’s stepping back from the fiscal cliff, in my mind the step was more of a
soft-shoe shuffle, if not a sidestep.
The US remains on the brink of a chasm. Despite an extension, in a few short months
the Department of the Treasury runs out of legal authority to borrow. Failure to raise the
so-called debt ceiling would force the US G overnment to default on its obligations, and
force immediate cuts equivalent to almost 6 percent of GDP. This could easily drive the
US back into recession. Is there cause  for alarm? In the summer of 2011 the
Republicans were solipsistic and cavalier in using the threat of default to extract
concessions from President Obama and the Democrats. As a result, one credit agency
stripped the US of its AAA rating, adding ro ils of further and largely unnecessary stress
to the foundations of the already shaky global financial system. If petty politics pertain
in the US, we could be in for more of the same.
Some economists at Davos expressed so me optimism regarding China, as its
economic slow-down seems less serious than a year ago, but challenges remain, as there
is a shift in focus from an export-driven  economy to one that relies on domestic
consumption. China’s vast reserve of cheap workers is dwindling rapidly, and it will not
be very long before China’s demographic dividend is spent.
Although Mario Draghi of the European Central Bank is trumpeting 2012 as the year
that the troubled single currency was relaunc hed, deep systemic failures—fault-lines—
run beneath the surface of the eurozone . Rising unemployment, a growing social
disconnect, declining competitiveness, and th e fundamental tension between integration
and sovereignty in times of austerity are becoming more and more evident.
This principled, pragmatic Government is  making the prudent financial decisions
necessary to weather the ongoing economic tu rbulence. No Government has a magic
wand to wave, and no Government can change things overnight. However, our balanced
approach of economic stimulus combined with deficit reduction is working, and
working well. It is worth reit erating that it attracted a ri nging endorsement from one of
US President Obama’s financial advisers, Pe ter Orszag, who was Obama’s director of
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7723
the Office of Management and Budget until 2010. He singled out New Zealand as the
model sans pareil for its balanced approach to the deepening international debt crisis.
New Zealand is the only c ountry in the world that has “coupled additional stimulus
with medium-term fiscal consolidation.” Just last week the interna tional credit agency
Moody’s in its latest cred it analysis of New Zeal and said the country’s AAA
Government bond rating reflected “high economic strength, very high institutionalised
and government financial strengt h and low susceptibility to ev ent risk.” That is sound
recognition of this Government’s strategy.
A society is judged by how it treats its most vulnerable.  This National-led
Government has borrowed to cushion vulnerable New Zealanders from the sharpest
edges of the recession, at the same time as ma intaining strong financial discipline. As a
result the New Zealand economy is performi ng better than that of the US, Japan,
countries of the eurozone such as Germa ny and France, and also the UK. We have
focused on growth that is sustainable and is  built on higher savings and earnings rather
than ever increasing debt.
How have we worked to protect the most vulnerable? Around $2 billion of
borrowing over the last 4 years has been us ed to protect and grow public health
services. This has contributed to the impr oved health services New Zealanders are
seeing every day, including free doctors’ vis its for children under 6 years, 35,000 more
New Zealanders getting elective surgery each year than 4 years ago, and record numbers
of patients being treated in emergency depa rtments within 6 hours.  But it is not only
that—hugely increased numbers of our chil dren are being vacc inated, and we are
aiming to do even better. We are increasing the target for infant immunisation rates to
95 percent of 8-month-olds being immunised with three scheduled vaccinations by
We regard the incidence of rheumatic feve r in some of our communities, including
the vibrant and diverse community of Ma nurewa where I have my office, as
unacceptable. We are investing $24 million and have set ourselves a target of reducing
the incidence of rheumatic fever by two-thirds by 2017. Delivering better services to the
public is one of our four key priorities. Ou r public services are steadily improving their
effectiveness to get the most out of every health dollar.
Attending a global health forum last year, I met many de legates who were
complaining that their Governments were cutting health spending. By contrast New
Zealand’s public heal th service is doing extraordinar ily well. In 2009-10, while other
OECD countries were reducing health spending, New Zealand had a 3.4 percent
increase in real health spend—the third-hi ghest of 27 nations. This is possible only
through prudent financial management and building a strong and competitive economy.
New Zealand is a trading nation. Build ing a more competitive and productive
economy for New Zealand provides the resource s necessary to protect the vulnerable in
society, maintain the rule of law, provide  high quality public se rvices—some of which
we have just mentioned—look after the e nvironment, and provide opportunities for our
young people. Trade is our lifeblood. About  2 weeks ago the OECD and the World
Trade Organization launched a new database of Trade in Value Added. This new data
estimates trade in value-added terms, which helps convey the interdependence of global
value chains and reveal who ultimately benefits.
New Zealand is especially well connected to global value chains in agriculture and
the food sector. The OECD estimates that 81 percent of New Zealan d exports’ value is
created domestically. This is higher than the OECD average of 72 percent and reflective
of both our geographic distan ces from market and the importance of agricultural
products to our exports. As the Minister of Trade, Tim Groser, pointed out, this
database provides an important reminder that  imports are vital to production of exports.
7724 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
About one-third of New Zealand imports of intermediate inputs are used to produce
goods and services that are then exported.
Now that we can quantify the contribution of imports to value-added exports, it
becomes clear that any barrier to imports in turn becomes a barrier to our exports and to
our firms engaging internationally. Countries  must ensure that business can access
world-class inputs at competitive prices if they are to be pr oductive and reap the benefit
from global value chains and trade. The economic shamans a nd rune readers on the left
constantly cry out for intervention to fo rce the dollar down. One is reminded of King
Canute—the cri de coeur from the economic sans-culottes is never accompanied by any
explanation of how this may be achieved without ruinous inflation. It betrays a touching
faith in the manifest abilities of our National-led Government that they believe us
capable of doing so.
It is worth knowing that Australia receives the bulk of our manufactured exports and
the New Zealand - Australian cross rate has never been more favourable in the last 10
years. Obviously, a strong kiwi dollar can provide a headwind to some New Zealand
exporters, but also, depending on the propor tion of imported inputs to the goods and
services, can be an aid to exporters. We constantly need to remind ourselves that
companies like Apple, Toyota, and indeed F onterra did not achieve their global success
through selling goods cheaper than anyone else.
The strong dollar has had other consequences. We ran a $486 million trade surplus in
December—the largest trade surplus recorded for the December month as a percentage
of exports in 21 years. The surplus is due in  part to the costs of imports coming down
because of the strong New Zealand dolla r. Taking out the big one-off items and
adjusting for exchange rate, imports were actually up 7 percent in the December quarter.
This, of course, suggests our economic recovery is continuing, and we may be in for a
pleasant surprise; an incr ease in the 0.4 percent Reserve Bank forecast when the
December quarter economic growth figures are released.
World dairy prices have improved in the December quarter and export prices are
turning up, which augurs well for 2013. A healthy, growing, sustainable economy
allows us, as I have mentioned, to prov ide a safe, secure environment in our
communities, high-quality public services, and the opportunities for our young people to
unlock the potential and creativity that lies w ithin them all, and to protect the most
vulnerable—in other words, a brighter future for all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I wish to acknowledge and
congratulate our Speaker, David Carter, on his role and wish him all the best in that
role. We look forward to seeing him progress in that position over the next few years.
This debate is a very important one, because  it sets out the philosophical differences
between the two political parties that represen t the two main parties of this Parliament.
On one side you have the National Party in Government with our great Prime Minister,
the Rt Hon John Key, doing the right thing by New Zealand, and on the other side you
have the Labour Party—a party of envy, a pa rty distraught in itself about who its
leadership actually is, a party that is looking for itself in the mirror but cannot find itself
there. Then on the heels of that you have th e smaller parties like New Zealand First and
the Green Party there. New Zealand First members are beaming at the thought of being
in Parliament for another 3 years. They do not actually care whether they do anything,
but just the fact that they  are here is enough for them. The Green Party members are
sitting there, diligent as ever, but completely  misrepresenting to the public what they
stand for and what they want for this country going forward.
It is a shame that politics becomes a battle of perceptions. We think in this
Parliament that it is a matter of  perception and it is  advertising. It is like Coke against
Pepsi, is it not—you know, National against Lab our—but it is not really that, actually.
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7725
The public out there are much smarter th an we think. They can see through the
perceptions and the facades on the other side . They know that the Labour Party and the
Green Party and the New Zealand First Party do  not actually stand for what is right for
New Zealanders. They know that those part ies will not do the right thing for this
country going forward, and they do not vote for them. It is that simple.
The public out there look beyond the percepti ons that this House tries to portray,
look at the realities of the policies, and determine that those Opposition parties do not
have a plan, they do not have the people, and they do not have the resources to actually
do what the people out there actually want. Wh at the people actually want is what this
Government is delivering. They want good, soli d management that is going to direct
this country through very difficult economic tim es. They want a Government that cares
about social, health, and education issues. They  want a Government th at is interested in
our people and, especially, in our young peopl e’s future. They want a country and a
Government that builds and builds a stronge r country going forward, so that future
generations of New Zealanders have the opportunities and the ability to live in a first-
class country going forward. They know they  are getting that from the National
Government. They voted us in because they knew our plan. They like it and they want
to keep it going.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: You tell this to the 50,000 going to Australia this year.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The New Zealand First Party keeps on talking about people
going to Australia. Well, that is the compe titive pressure that we have. You know, we
cannot avoid it.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: 50,000 a year. It’s the only reason why they’re not staying here.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: We live right beside Australi a, that is right. We have a
competitive pressure there. But that means that New Zealanders and the New Zealand
Government have to step up. The Opposition wants to do exactly the opposite. The New
Zealand First Party wants to create Fort ress New Zealand. It does not want anybody
coming into New Zealand and it does not want anybody leaving New Zealand. It just
sees New Zealand as a fortress that will survive.  Well, that is completely irrational. It is
not going to happen. It has never happened in world history.
The Labour Party, on the other hand, is saying: “Well, why aren’t you doing
something? What are you doing?”. Well, we ha ve got a plan, and the plan is something
that the public sees. It is about investing in this country going forward.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: It’s a cunning plan. Nobody knows what it is.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: You want to see the plan? I wi ll tell you about the plan. Come
to Hamilton and you will see the plan, because Hamilton is going ahead and it is doing
really well. Do you know why it is going ahead?

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: That’s because it’s getting a bypass.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It is getting a bypass—exactl y. The New Zealand First Party
gets 10 points. A golden star to the New Z ealand First Party for getting it right. The
Government is building the infrastructure that enables Hamilton to take advantage of its
biggest opportunity, which is Auckland. It is linking Hamilton to Auckland, just like
New Zealand needs to link with Asia. Our oppor tunity in the future  comes from those
big Asian economies that will direct a lot of mone y around this part of  the world. If we
do not link into those countries, we will miss out on our opportunity.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Skycity Casino.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Skycity Casino is another thi ng that the New Zealand First
Party does not want to see happen. It brings jobs into New Zealand, but you do not want
to see it happen.
When we look at it, the issue that the La bour Party and the Opposition have tried to
promote over the last couple of months has b een housing. That is wh at they have been
7726 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
saying. They have been pushing the housing but ton. Well, let us have a look at it. We
live on the Pacific Rim, beside the countries that will be the richest on this planet for the
next 100 years—Australia, China, Viet Nam,  the Philippines, and Indonesia. Those are
the countries that will pump out the wealth of this world for the next 100 years. If the
New Zealand public and the Opposition think that  there will not be some impact on the
New Zealand economy from being right beside those countries, then we are being naive.
We will need to be able to play the game w ith those countries. We will need to be able
to have a world-class education system, so that our young people can grow up and
compete.
We will have to compete on our assets, as well. We will have to pay the price for
housing. There will be no free rides in this world. There is no fortress mentality where
you can say that New Zealand lives in a differe nt world. We want to be in that world.
We want to be in a world where our childre n can aspire to getting good jobs, can aspire
to getting a good income, and can aspire to having their own home, because in that way
they will be living the First World dream. If we do not aspire to that, if we think that we
can dumb our economy down, if we think that we can dumb our people down, and if we
think that we can deliver houses for $300,000, then you are dreaming. Get in the real
world.
We need to compete. That is the challe nge that New Zealande rs understand. That is
the challenge that the New Zealand Nationa l Government understands. That is the
challenge that the Opposition denies. It denies  the challenge of this world and it denies
the challenge of our people. That is why it will suffer in  the polls in 2014—because it
does not understand the realit y of what our people are go ing through and the challenges
in front of our country.
But do not look at it as a challenge. It is not a challenge; it is an opportunity, because
the real opportunity for us is  to succeed. If we succeed with  those countries in the next
100 years, New Zealand can be on e of the wealthiest countries  in the world. That is the
crossroads we have in front of us now: to accept the challenge and succeed, or to try to
put up some walls and say: “It’s too hard. We’re not part of that.” That is the choice that
the public has out there.
We have young people watching from the ga llery today. They have that choice
today. Their choice is to get a good education and make the most of their opportunities,
or to not get a good education and think that it is going to come their way. Well, it is a
different world from when we  all grew up. The world that you grow up in will not give
you that choice. You will have to make the right choices, and that involves getting that
education and doing that hard work, because  there will be no second chance. The
Opposition believes that there is some pot of gold that will suddenly deliver that for
them.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: On the bypass—it’s on the bypass.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The New Zealand First Party ta lks about the bypass. Well, that
is linking Hamilton to Auckland, like New Zealand will be linked to China and those
other countries going forward. Hamilton is  doing well, because we understand the
future. We are not afraid to take those challenges. We have invested in those challenges.
We have put money into broadband, we ha ve put money into the university, and we
have put money into the hospital—we have  put money into the infrastructure. My
colleagues from the north look with envy on us, but we have done it and we are
succeeding. That is the future of New Zealand, just like it is the future of my city. I look
forward to this Government carrying on throu gh this term and delivering that future. It
is a strong future, it is the ri ght future, and it is the only future that will enable our
younger generations to actually succeed in the modern world. Thank you.
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7727

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: May I express to you, Mr Deputy Speaker, a
happy new parliamentary year. I also jo in other parliamentary colleagues in
congratulating our new Speaker, the Rt Hon Da vid Carter. We wish him all the best in
his new role. We have seen his first outing as Speaker in his first question time today,
and I think we will give him a provisional pass—it used to be a C- back in the fifth
form, a provisional pass. We wish him all the be st in that new challenge. I know he is a
Canterbury man, born and bred, so he has what it takes to be able to succeed in that role.
Can I also wish members of the House a happy New Year too.
I apologise to those people watching at hom e, because they have just had to put up
with three speakers from the National Party— that is 30 minutes uninterrupted of
absolute spin and drivel from the Governme nt. We heard that from the last speaker,
David Bennett from Hamilton. Hamilton is a lo vely place. I have got nothing against it,
other than what the MP for Hamilton East has just said. He said that this debate is
important because it is a philosophical debate  about what our party stands for and what
their party stands for, and he is absolute ly 100 percent correct in  that. I cannot agree
more with what Rodney Hide said about the Government when he was in this House:
this is a do-nothing Government . It is a do-nothing Governme nt, and we have seen that
for the last 4 years.
And then Cam Calder, earlier, talked a bout judging a country on how it treats its
vulnerable. I want to talk a l ittle bit about that, because, Mr  Calder, one vulnerable part
of our society is the Pacifi c Island community. If you want  to talk about how that
Government’s track record over the last 4 years has gone about looking after that
vulnerable community, last week when the unemployment statistics came out we saw
that 16 percent of Pacific people are unemp loyed—16 percent. That is, roughly one in
eight of the Pacific people in  this country who want work have no work. Let us look at
that track record over the la st 4 years. It has gone from  15.6 to 16 percent—so, another
rise in the last quarter. At this time last year the Pacifi c unemployment rate was 13.8
percent. So how is this Government looki ng after the Pacific community, when in the
last 12 months it has looked after the vulne rable Pacific Island community by letting
unemployment go up by 2.2 percent? How is that Government going to be judged by
the Pacific community when it looks it in the face in 2014 and says “We’ve looked after
you. You’re a vulnerable community.”? You ha ve not. You have not one iota, because
16 percent is more than twice—more than twice—the current average national
unemployment rate. So when that member of Parliament says “We’ve looked after
vulnerable communities.”, you have not, and especially not the Pacific community.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I am sorry, Mr Deputy Speaker. This Government has not; it has
not looked after the Pacific community.
We are talking about the Prime Minister’s statement, and, you know, the brave effort
that he made. I thought it was not his best—po tentially his worst. But I want to know
what has happened to the old John Key. What  has happened to the old John Key? Back
in 2008, and before that, he was positive about our country. He used to say “We’re
aspirational for a brighter future. We’re tu rbocharging. We’re kicking the tyres.” But
that John Key has gone. That John Key has gone. We have seen someone who said he
stood on principle—and then Mr Bennett says th at voters want to know what this party
stands for. I think it is clear to see that the people of New Zealand know that the
National Party stands for whatever the last focus group said. The people of New
Zealand know that this National Government stands for whatever the last focus group
said. So where is the old John Key? The “Shucks!”, happy-go-lu cky Prime Minister
whom the people of New Zealand thought was the be-all and end-all and would change
the future of this Government—a man who said he was going to be a leader for New
7728 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
Zealand to a brighter future but who has b ecome only a manager of a bleak present. He
said this pretty soon after he came into power: New Zealand woul d be coming out of
recession “reasonably aggressively” by early 2010. So New Zealand would come out of
the recession “reasonably aggressively” by ear ly 2010. Well, one measure of that is our
unemployment level, and it is still—still—much, much higher. And I think it was
Steven Joyce, at question time, who starte d patting himself on the back because last
Thursday the unemployment rate went from 7.3 percent to 6.8 percent.
But let us do something that the National Part y hates, and let us look at the facts. Let
us look at the facts. When those figures cam e out it was very interesting to read, and a
very helpful lady at Statistics New Zeala nd, the industry and labour statistics manager
Diane Ramsay, said: “We’re seeing fewer people working and looking for work, and
more people outside the labour force. More younger people are solely in study and more
older people are entering retirement,”. So, basically, what she is saying, in her statistical
frame, is that it is bleak out there for most New Zealanders. It is bleak out there for most
New Zealanders. And the sad th ing about that is that when  she is saying that fewer
people are looking for work, she is saying they have lost hope that they can find work.
They have lost hope that they can find wo rk. This Government will be worried about
that because when people start losing hope that they can find work, that is going to start
really impacting the Government, and I think that will really impact it over the next 12
months.
As the MP for Mana I want to take a bit of  a closer look at those figures, take a
closer-to-home look at those figures, b ecause Wellington unemployment is at an 18-
year high. Wellington unemployment is at an 18-year high. Not since 1994 has it been
worse. It went from 7.1 percent in the September quarter to 7.9 percent in the December
quarter—1 percent higher than the national average. Basically, the raw numbers are that
there are 22,600 unemployed people in the Wellington region, and in the previous
quarter there were 21,000. So 1,600 more people in this region, in our capital, are now
unemployed compared with the previous 3 months. Again, thos e are people who are
losing hope that they can get a job, and losing hope that this Government can do
anything to help them to try to find a job. Those New Zealanders are the forgotten New
Zealanders whom National does not care  about any more—whom National does not
care about any more. Kiwis across the country are working harder than ever. They are
doing their fair share. They ar e either working or looking for work, but they feel let
down by this Government, which promised them a brighter future. Where is this
brighter future? This is a Government that has forgo tten about those people—those
people who have gone off the register, who are no longer looking for work. It is only a
Labour-led Government that will stand up for those hard -working Kiwis whom this
Government has forgotten.
As I said before, this is a do-nothing Government, and in 2014 the people of New
Zealand will elect a hands-on approach that will be different from what this
Government has done. This Government has been a do-nothing, let-the-market-decide
Government. Well, that has not worked for th e last 4 years, and you can feel the sense
of unease that the people of New Zealand put faith in that Government, in that party,
that things would turn round, and all they ge t is excuses and more excuses that things
have not. There needs to be a new era here in New Zealand, and th at is what we are
promising in terms of a hands-on Government. We need a smart, hands-on Government,
and a Government that is prepared to be a player and not a spectator.
I think one of the best ways that we have done that—and we actually promised this at
the last election—is we are going to help  our young people, whom Mr Bennett claims
he was going to help. We on this side of the House have been saying that
apprenticeships have been a priority for a lot longer than this party, which thought it
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7729
was a good idea in early January because the focus group said so. Back in 2011, when
we put out our policy, we basically said that we would make an investment in our young
people who wanted to upskill and get into  work, and we would help those people—
those chippies, those plumbers, those electricians who needed help with an extra pair of
hands—by having a policy of making sure that we turn the dole into a subsidy for those
employers that need an apprentice. A nd when we go around—and I was speaking to a
builder in my electorate the other day—they love that idea . They love that idea, and
they do not necessarily buy wh at the Government is doi ng at the moment: coming up
late to this party, saying that apprentices hips, all of a sudden, are important to the
Government. This Government has done very l ittle around jobs for th e last 4 years, and
then all of a sudden—

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: Rubbish.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: He calls it rubbish, but look at the figures. Look at the figures. The
figures do not lie, Mr Woodhouse. The figures do not lie, and the people know what is
going on there. When you come late to th e party around apprenticeships, people will
notice that. People will notice that. Our policy of turning the dole into a subsidy for
employers is a good thing for those young people whom Mr Bennett says he cares
about, but also a good thing for those employers that are str uggling, that need an extra
set of hands, and that would love to take on somebody but cannot quite make the
commitment because it is too much of a financial barrier. So that is one of the hands-on
things that we are going to do. That is not stand-offish. That is not letting the market
decide. That is a hands-on approach.
And then you look at our KiwiBuild  scheme—100,000 homes over 10 years to
address not only the employment problem but  also the housing affordability problem,
which this Government has done nothing ab out. Its only answ er to the housing
affordability problem is to make Nick Smith in charge of it. Is this some kind of joke?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Can I begin by
thanking members of the House and those others who acknowledged and congratulated
me on my promotion a couple of weeks ago. It has certainly been a very hectic and busy
time, and I am looking forward to the challeng es those portfolios hold. I also want to
acknowledge my former junior whip, now th e chief whip for the Government, Louise
Upston, and her new team of Tim Macindoe a nd No. 3, “The Whippet”, Jami-Lee Ross.
I am sure they will be a tremendous team and continue to keep the caucus energised.
If there was any theme that underpinned Christmas 2012 for me it was the theme of
the Christmas hamper. Of course, many ha mpers were given out , but I think the
interesting thing for me was the one that  was not. There was an article in the Otago
Daily Times that rather warmed me, actually, through the very challenging period of the
closure of the Hillside railway workshops—at least, that part that was not taken up by
Bradken—and the work that local MP Clare Curran did to provide hampers for what
was believed to be all the workers at Hillside. Indeed, she was quoted in the Otago
Daily Times saying that “she called for donations of hamper items for Hillside staff, and
said yesterday ‘hundreds’ of products ha d come in from Dunedin businesses and
individuals since the appeal  was launched”—businesses th at I think thought would be
donating to all KiwiRail workers who were affected by this cl osure. But apparently not,
because one member was not given a hamper, and that member had something that the
others did not. He was not a member of th e trade union. In fact, he was quoted in the

items.speaker: Otago Daily Times as saying
items.text: “I asked if there was a hamper for me and was told no,”—

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Make sure you get the facts right, Michael.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: —these are the facts as reported by the Otago
Daily Times —“because I was a National supporter  and a scabber. The union people
simply don’t want me to have a hamper becau se I voted National and always have.” So
7730 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
those Dunedin businesses were not donating to Hillside workers; they were donating to
union workers. Clare Curran cries tears not for Kiwi workers but for her union mates,
because when she had an opportunity to say that this was a mistake and that clearly
there was a misunderstanding about who would get the hampers, she did not.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: I seek leave to make a personal explanation.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No. Order! The time to do that is between when
members have the call. It is not a mechanis m to interrupt a speaker. I will not put the
leave, but that is not saying that the memb er cannot do it. I am informing the member
when she can do it.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I fear I have touched a
nerve. However, there was an opportunity to say that this was a misunderstanding.
There was an opportunity to co rrect this, but, ra ther, Miss Curran was quoted in the
Otago Daily Times  saying that “She ‘understood’  some workers would not get
hampers”—“some”, notice, not “one”—“but said she did not ask why, and did not know
whether hampers were given only to union members. She sa id she would not be taking
any action.” Well, I know what the public of Dunedin thought about that, concerned
though they were at the closure of the Hillside railway workshops. There was disgust on
social media at the perceptions of that action.
But roll on the new year, and we have last week’s decision by the Auditor-General to
not, unlike what Ms Curran had requested, cond uct a further inquiry into the purchase
of flat-deck wagons by KiwiRail. I note the Office of the Auditor-General basically said
“We have concluded that the decision to sele ct CNR as a supplier was made for normal
business and commercial reasons after a compet itive market process.” This happens to
be exactly what KiwiRail was required to  do under section 4 of the State-Owned
Enterprises Act, an Act passed by a Labour G overnment. It could have amended it, but
it did not. Section 4 says that there was a requirement to adopt normal commercial
practice. But the Office of the Auditor-Gener al goes on to say “We did not identify any
unfairness in the way the proposal from Hillside workshops was treated.”, and it
concluded—significantly, I shou ld say, for me—by saying “we have seen no evidence
to suggest improper influence over these deci sions.” So, no influence, and KiwiRail did
exactly what it was required to do: follow normal commercial practice, invite Hillside to
submit a bid, which it came a distant third on, and make a commercial decision that an
Act passed by a Labour Government required it to do.
The only person prepared to stand up and sa y that they would change that law was
Clare Curran. Phil Goff, when he was Leader of the Opposition, came down and said he
would not change the law. He said “We’d look into it. We’d give Kiwis a go.”—and,
absolutely, that is required in any event. Da vid Shearer stopped short of saying that he
would change the law, but Clare Curran said: “Nope. Under a Labour Government we’d
reopen Hillside. We’d give them the subsid ies that they would need. We would take
$160 million, by conservative estimates, out of the pockets of hard-working taxpayers
to fund that project, because, unfort unately, Hillside was not big enough or
technological enough to compete on the wo rld market.” So there it is—$160 million
more in subsidies, and heaven knows what else would come our way.
It is tough out there in manufacturing. It  is not a crisis, but it is tough. This
Government does not have the luxury, howev er, of only talking about the negatives.
There is job growth. I happened to visit Bradken yesterday morning. Bradken purchased
the foundry at the Hillside railway works hops, and, in fact, its admin officers were
moving into Hillside Road just this morning, so  I was very grateful to them that they
accommodated me. And they are upbeat. There is new work, there are new jobs being
created, there are plenty of opportunities for the big pots th at it has there to do foundry
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7731
work under one tonne, and it coul d become Australasia’s leader in that market. So there
is cause for optimism.
I just want to touch on some of those ne w responsibilities that I have as, firstly,
Minister of Immigration, which perhaps on the face of it would seem like a rather dry
portfolio. But I am very excited by it, because it is an absolutely vital cog in the wheel
of the Government’s Business Growth Agenda . New Zealand is in a contest—a global
contest—for talent, for tertiary students, for tourists, and for migrants who are prepared
to invest in this country. I have been really, really enc ouraged by the manner in which
Immigration New Zealand has improved over the last 4 years, and there are strategies
under way that will supercharge that organisation and ensure that the skilled migrants
that we need in order to take that Business Growth Agenda forward will be here.
I want to touch on one small matter that has been raised over the last few days in
respect of the immigration portfolio, and that  is the issue of asylum seekers and the
passage of the Immigration Amendment Bill, which is due for its second reading soon. I
have been asked—and it has been claimed even  in this House during oral question time
that there is no risk, and that  it would be completely impossible for a boat to get from
Indonesia, for example, to New Zealand. Well, I want to remind the House that most of
our ancestors arrived here in sail ships and waka.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How many refugees have been found in waka?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: And anybody who thinks that a steel-hulled,
motorised vessel with a number of peopl e—dozens or hundreds—could not make New
Zealand shores is, frankly, being naive. And I challenge Andrew Little to be saying the
same thing if and when that event occurs, beca use the risk is real, the possibility is real,
and the response is necessary.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: No, it’s not.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, there we go. We have it on record. Mr
Little says “No, it’s not real.” Thank you. I shall mark the date and time, because the
risk is real and if Labour does not believe so, well, we will just see.
I want to just finish  on the issue of vetera ns’ affairs. This is a very busy year for
veterans’ affairs. Planning for the 100 th anniversary commemorations of Gallipoli,
begun under the previous veterans’ affairs Minister, the Hon Nathan Guy, is well under
way. There will be an announcement very so on, if not already, on the allocation of
places for New Zealanders and Australians to  that event. There are also a number of
other commemorations taking place this year that are going to be very important: the
70th anniversary of the war in  the North Pacific, the 60 th anniversary of the signing of
the ceasefire in Korea, and, of course, we have the very important work that veterans are
looking for in the rewrite of the War Pensi ons Act 1954. So I can tell you it is going to
be an extremely busy year. I look forward to all of those things ta king place as part of
the important work this Government will be doing.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: I seek leave to make a personal
explanation in response to comments made about me by the previous speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: It must be personal comments, to
you personally. Leave is sought for that purpos e. Is there any objection? There is no
objection.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: I think it is important to put the correct facts into the Hansard
around the donation of materials for Christma s hampers to the Hillside workers and my
part in that before Christmas. There were  112 hampers put together. More than $18,000
worth of goods was donated by dozens of local businesses, which I organised, and, as I
said, 112 hampers were produced. Not all of the people given those hampers were union
members. Quite a number of them were not union members, and there were certainly
more than 112 people still at Hillside. The list of people whom those donated hampers
7732 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
were given to was certainly drawn up by the un ion delegates, who gave me that list, and
I was unquestioning in that because that was their right. As you can imagine, there was
a lot of emotion at the Hillside railway work shops before Christmas, as 90 people lost
their jobs due to the prioritisation by this Government of lowest cost—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member can relate only
how you were personally affected by the co mments that were being made. You cannot
get into debate. Has the member finished?

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Not quite. I certainly think that there is relevance here, because
the previous speaker, Mr Woodhouse, has ma de comments about the unfairness of one
particular person—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, look—[Interruption] Order! A
personal statement is your response to be able  to put your position. This is not a debate;
it is about how the comments made by a prev ious speaker have affected you personally.
That is your right and you ha ve got leave to do that, but  you cannot then get into a
debate about the substance of that. So I as k the member to be very succinct on this,
because otherwise I will close it down.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Thanks, Mr Speaker. Certainly it had an effect on me—having
the wrong facts put into the Hansard by the member across the House. There were
certainly many people who received Christma s hampers who were not union members,
and there was certainly more than one pers on who did not receive a hamper for very
good reasons. Thank you.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: I would just like to take an opportunity to
congratulate our new Speaker. I hope that we can have a great relationship with him and
that the opportunity of free speech in this pr esent Parliament will be upheld by all of us
for the benefit of all of us as an important right that should be protected by all Speakers
and also by all MPs, irrespective of the political bias of any political party.
I would also like to acknowle dge that the debate on the Prime Minister’s statement
came at the end of a beautiful summer, but after that I slightly lost my will to live. I find
my will to live struggling when we listen to motherhood and apple pie, which we can all
agree with, but underneath it the ideology, the rhetoric, and the attempt to justify the
attack on education in the Prime Ministe r’s speech, but also in the Minister of
Education’s speech, were quite notable. The Prime Minister’s speech was focusing on
national standards as the only—and d eeply unpopular—method by which educational
outcomes are going to be changed. Hekia Para ta’s speech was very defensive. It was
understandably defensive because there are so many debacles on the list.
I want to talk a bit about the debacles but also about the positive vision, because out
there, outside the beltway, th ere are some fantastic people  working in education who
absolutely believe in quality, public, local education. I had the privilege of attending a
hui at Waitangi for engaging Māori learners, which occurs every year. It is a conference
of teachers and principals not only in Northland but often Northlanders. They were very
welcoming because what they are really interested in is how  quality, local, self-
managing schools with a good relationship with  the Government can  actually achieve
the goals of supporting their young people.
We have schools such as Moerewa School, where Ngāti Hine have worked so hard to
make a curriculum based on their own communi ty’s desires for how their children will
become good citizens, and then the school is cut off at th e knees by Government policy
and by Government action. It was distressing to see people from that community in
tears while talking about the lo ss of their children. What ha s happened is that with the
axing of the school’s senior class, which was being taught in Te Reo, we have lost
young people from the system. We have lost  young people who did not want to go to
other schools and who now have had the message that the Government does not want
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7733
them to be part of education on their own community’s terms. A punitive approach to
education and towards schools that have an aspiration—a favourite Government word—
for their own children to be educated accordin g to their own beliefs has been lost, and
that is a very sad thing.
I could also pick on Wanganui Collegiate School, if I felt like it. It is really tempting.
My partner went there, and he has got some  interesting things to say about it. The
Government is certainly spending a lot of m oney on it, bailing it out to the tune of $3
million a year through integration, because that school cannot stand on its own feet. But
it is still going to charge thous ands of dollars of fees and we are going to help pay for
that—a very bizarre scenario. When you lo ok at the deed of Wanganui Collegiate
School in 1852, Sir George Grey actually said that the school was to benefit Europeans
and Māori. And if you look furthe r down the deed, you will se e—and this is something
my partner has often quoted to  me—that it was supposed to be for the poor of Aotearoa
and the Pacific and M āori, as well as Europeans. Inst ead of which we have a private
school that has now been bailed out, which is going to cost the taxpayer at just the time
when the Christchurch schools are facing tr emendous stress about their viability—and
that announcement is coming up really soon.
We are talking about Wanganui Collegi ate School, Novopay, national standards,
charter schools, and early childhood education fees going up because of the targeting of
people who are 100 percent qualified. I met somebody this weekend in Invercargill who
lost her job because she was qualified. That is the kind of perverse incentive for any
country that wants to build a stable, strong, viable system where all our children have
access to a quality, creative, participatory education system, when somebody in early
childhood education loses their job not becau se they are not good at their job but
because the early childhood centre, under this Government, cannot afford to hire them
any more. That consequence will ripple thr ough the generations, because our smallest
people need our best. Just because they do not vote doe s not mean we should not focus
our attention on the smallest people. They need the quality teaching and the quality
support, instead of which we have a priva tised sector where the not-for-profits are
struggling and with baby barns, where the babi es are lined up and all have their nappies
changed at the same time. That kind of robotic universe prepared for some kind of weird
production line is not the future for early childhood education.
If you look at Te Wh āriki, which is a fantastic curriculu m, there is now pressure that
there should be more assessment of childre n. So in early childhood education we are
going from portfolios and the idea of child-centred integrated learning to the idea that
we need to have more assessment like national standards for 3-year-olds. That will
really work, because it is really not work ing in schools. There is an alternative to
national standards, and that is actually called trust. It  is called trusting schools and
trusting parents to actually develop a curricu lum that works, and to stick within the
broad parameters of a very good curriculum, instead of imagining that measuring is
going to work. Instead of actually feeding the cow, as they say in Canada, it is about
weighing the cow. No matter how often you we igh things, especially if you weigh them
differently in every community, you are not going to end up with any information that is
going to be worth having about how to improve the so-called long tail of
underachievement.
I would never belittl e the reality for children w ho are struggling in our school
system. I would never be little that. That is why at the Engaging M āori Learners
Conference we heard from principals a nd teachers who are actually innovating. They
are not measuring, they are not  labelling, they are not puttin g on their website, they are
not competing, they are not tr ying to be privatised, they do not want to be charter
schools, they do not want to have secret c ontracts, and they do not want unregistered
7734 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2013
teachers. Actually, what they want to do is ma ke sure that they are meeting the goals of
the families and wh ānau of their communities in terms of actually making our teachers
able to be culturally inclusive and responsive.
What we have is Te Kotahitanga—one  of the most culturally responsive
programmes—which allows P ākehā teachers to become reflec tive practitioners on their
bias against Māori children.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How can you say you’ve got a bi as? How can you say you’ve got a
bias?

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: It has been blocked. Forty-four schools have seen
great success. One in Hamilton, which the member from Hamilton may not know about,
saw National Certificate of Educational Achi evement results go from  23 percent to 77
percent. That happened because of Te Ko tahitanga, because of the fact of that
programme, and the Government has limited it to 44 schools. It has cut it. It has been
limited because the Government thinks it might cost money. I am speaking about the
importance of Ka Hikitia—Managing for Success and Te Kotahitanga as instruments of
allowing teachers to reflect on their own practic e, and when you have that instrument
blocked, you have got to ask why and what the alternative is.
National standards versus proper professional development of teachers is a very, very
sad thing, because what we are seeing is that proper professional development has been
sacrificed. Everything has b een sacrificed to national standards. The Government
Budget has been sacrificed to narrowing the curriculum. Science advisers, drama
advisers, all of those advisers who have lost positions are constantly contacting the
Greens and saying that a broad curriculum allows a child to learn differently. It may be
news to some people, but all kids start at different stages. Some talk when they are 2,
some talk when they are 3 months—I was one  of those—some talk when they are 4,
some cannot stop talking. The fact is that they all develop at their own rate, and so when
you start trying to measure them and put them  in boxes, and when you start saying that
the only pathway to literacy is through lit eracy—rather than through drama for some
kids, it is through science fo r others, it is through E nviroschools for others—you have
narrowed the curriculum. Nati onal standards—everyone knows they are not national or
a standard, so that is another sad debacle. In hindsight, as we ha ve heard from Hekia
Parata quite a bit lately, national standards will be another of those jokes.
Moving right along to the education amendment bill that is before the House at the
moment, it is reflected by the Government’s  commitment in the Prime Minister’s
speech that these are going to be the solutions . Privatisation is the solution to inequity.
The trickle-down theory was introduced in the 1980s by former members of this House,
with disastrous consequences for people w ho did not happen to be at the top, and who
happened to be trickled down upon. So th e trickled down upon will now have the
opportunity to go to schools with no register ed teachers if those sc hools desire. That is
an extraordinary response, but it is not a local one. Unfortunately, it is part of what we
call the GERM—the global education reform  movement—which is the neo-liberal
fight-back, because in education early childho od is being privatised , tertiary is being
privatised, and there is one thing left: the sc hool system. So let us do it. Let us take the
school system and privatise it and let us say that choice, the mantra of choice, is actually
about the mantra of privilege. You have only to talk to people from New Orleans who
actually saw the consequences of Hurricane Ka trina with the loss of their schools to see
that the privatising agenda, which is drivin g the Government’s education policy, is not
going to be a vision for a healthy, happy, just, and equitable community. The Green
Party has a much better vision. Kia ora koutou katoa.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: It has been very interesting sitting here listening to
National Party members giving their speeches on  the Prime Minister’s statement. It has
12 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7735
been basically spin and rhetoric and meani ngless drivel constantly all afternoon. I think
that if members of Mr Key’s own caucus are un able to elucidate exactly what his vision
and his plan are for New Zealand, then the rest of us do not really stand a chance. This
is the fifth year of this National-led Govern ment and we have been saying since the day
it was elected: “Show us the plan. Where is the grand plan for our economy? Where are
the jobs going to come from? Where are the ideas? Where is the vision of this John Key
- led National Government?”. Here we are, 5 years down the track, and still no answer.
There was a lot of apportioning of blam e from Mr Key and from National Party
members, a lot of telling us whose fault it was and who should have done this and who
should have done that, and a lot of trying to blame the previous Labour Government,
saying that the previous Labour Government is  to blame for the financial difficulties of
today, despite the fact that the previous La bour Government reduced net debt to zero,
paid off the debt, and ran surpluses ev ery year. The IMF, not a loony left-wing
organisation by any stretch, actu ally said that New Zealand was one of the best-placed
countries in the world to go through that gl obal financial crisis relatively unscathed
compared with other countries, because we had been prudent, we had reduced debt, and
we were in a position where the Government could get in and play its role in supporting
its economy and in supporting its communitie s and its families when times were
